one_line: Super-resolving images before segmentation improves mask plausibility while decreasing fidelity to the true scene, because predicted boundaries snap to hallucinated edges.
problem: SR preprocessing is routinely added ahead of segmentation for low-resolution inputs and evaluated by aggregate mIoU, without testing whether the gains reflect recovery of the true scene or agreement with generator-invented structure.
core_hypothesis: SR output pulls segmentation boundaries toward edges the generator invented; agreement with the ground truth of the true high-resolution scene degrades in locally ambiguous regions even as boundary smoothness and plausibility improve.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired LR/HR datasets, boundary F-score of SR-then-segment will be lower than segment-LR-then-upsample-mask specifically in regions of high SR residual (where SR output diverges most from true HR), with error magnitude increasing monotonically with local residual.
why_important: SR preprocessing is being adopted operationally in satellite, surveillance, and medical pipelines; if boundaries are systematically displaced toward fabricated evidence, downstream area and length measurements are biased rather than merely noisy, and more data will not fix it.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: SR utility is usually reported as aggregate metric change; conditioning boundary displacement on local SR residual magnitude as an explicit mechanism test appears less explored, pending literature search.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one paired LR/HR segmentation dataset, run one pretrained SR model and one frozen segmenter both ways, stratify boundary displacement by local SR residual, and test for the predicted monotonic relation.
main_risk: SR residual correlates with intrinsic scene difficulty, confounding the stratification; matched-difficulty controls or residual manipulation at fixed content are needed.
default_community_belief: SR preprocessing is a safe, generally beneficial enhancement step for low-resolution segmentation inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern segmenters may rely mostly on mid-frequency shape cues and ignore the high-frequency detail SR fabricates, making the displacement effect negligible in practice.
fastest_falsification: Half-day analysis with off-the-shelf SR and segmenter on one paired dataset; no training required.

one_line: MMSE-optimal denoising selectively erases low-contrast thin structures, so denoising can raise PSNR while lowering thin-class segmentation recall.
problem: Denoisers are trained to minimize mean squared error, which drives ambiguous low-SNR content toward the local mean; whether this systematically deletes the faint thin structures (wires, vessels, cracks) that segmentation needs is rarely quantified.
core_hypothesis: For structures whose contrast is near or below the noise floor, MMSE denoising is equivalent to structure deletion; segmentation recall on thin classes therefore drops after denoising even when full-image PSNR and SSIM improve.
falsifiable_prediction: Across noise levels, thin-structure recall of a frozen segmenter will be higher on noisy inputs than on denoised inputs once structure contrast falls below a measurable multiple of the noise sigma, while large-object IoU shows the opposite ordering.
why_important: Denoising is treated as a monotone quality improvement; a contrast-dependent deletion regime would mean preprocessing choices silently trade thin-class recall for cosmetic quality in safety-relevant pipelines like vessel and crack inspection.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the MMSE-attenuation argument is classical signal processing, but a quantitative deletion threshold expressed in units of structure contrast over noise sigma, validated against segmentation recall, appears not to be standard practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize thin structures at controlled contrast into real noisy backgrounds, denoise with two standard models, and plot segmenter recall versus contrast-to-noise ratio for noisy versus denoised inputs.
main_risk: Synthetic insertions may not capture real thin-structure statistics; a follow-up on a real vessel or crack dataset with noise added is needed for external validity.
default_community_belief: Denoising strictly helps downstream analysis whenever the input is visibly noisy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenters trained with heavy augmentation may already fail on sub-noise-floor structures, so denoising would remove nothing the model could use anyway.
fastest_falsification: One-day synthetic contrast-sweep experiment with pretrained denoisers and a pretrained segmenter.

one_line: Restoration models pretrained on natural images impose natural-scene priors that misinterpret domain-specific structures as artifacts and remove them.
problem: Off-the-shelf restoration models are increasingly applied to scientific and industrial imagery whose statistics differ from natural photographs, but the direction of the induced bias is not characterized.
core_hypothesis: Structures that are rare in natural-image statistics (isolated bright puncta, periodic grids, hairline defects) are treated by natural-image-trained restorers as noise or artifact and are attenuated or regularized away, with the attenuation predictable from the structure's likelihood under a natural-image prior.
falsifiable_prediction: Attenuation of inserted structures after restoration will correlate with their improbability under a natural-image density model, and segmentation recall for those structure classes will drop more than for natural-looking classes at matched size and contrast.
why_important: It converts anecdotes about restoration harming scientific images into a predictive law: which structures are at risk can be computed before deployment, enabling principled go/no-go decisions for restoration preprocessing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: linking per-structure restoration attenuation to an explicit likelihood score under a generative natural-image model, rather than reporting domain-level degradation, appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert structure families of varying natural-image likelihood into photographs at matched contrast, restore with pretrained models, and regress attenuation against likelihood scores from an independent density model.
main_risk: Density estimates from available generative models may be too unreliable at patch level to give a usable likelihood axis.
default_community_belief: Restoration failures on out-of-domain imagery are unpredictable domain-gap effects to be fixed by fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attenuation may be driven by local frequency content alone rather than semantic likelihood, in which case a simple spectral account beats the prior-likelihood account.
fastest_falsification: Compare attenuation predictions of a spectral baseline versus a likelihood model on one structure-insertion benchmark; if spectral wins, the hypothesis dies.

one_line: Jointly trained restoration-plus-segmentation systems pass segmentation hints through the restored image as imperceptible signals rather than genuinely improving image quality.
problem: End-to-end pipelines that train a restoration front-end with a downstream segmentation loss report gains, but the mechanism is assumed to be better image quality rather than covert channel coding between the two networks.
core_hypothesis: The restoration module learns to embed segmentation-relevant side information as low-amplitude patterns tuned to its paired segmenter, analogous to reported steganographic behavior in image-to-image translation; the restored images are not better inputs for independent segmenters.
falsifiable_prediction: Restored images from a jointly trained front-end will improve the paired segmenter substantially but transfer little or no gain to an independent frozen segmenter, and adding low-pass filtering or mild noise to the restored image will destroy the paired gain disproportionately.
why_important: If gains come from a cheating channel, joint restoration modules will fail silently whenever the downstream model is swapped or retrained, which is exactly how such pipelines are deployed in practice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: steganographic collusion is discussed for cycle-consistent translation; a targeted test in restoration-for-segmentation pipelines with transfer and perturbation controls appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a small restoration front-end jointly with segmenter A, then evaluate its outputs with frozen segmenters B and C and under mild perturbations; compare gain retention across the three conditions.
main_risk: Genuine task-tuned enhancement can also transfer poorly if segmenters differ in input statistics; the perturbation-sensitivity control is essential to separate the two explanations.
default_community_belief: Task-driven restoration gains reflect improved effective image quality for the task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The observed gains may survive perturbation and transfer, indicating genuine task-relevant enhancement rather than collusion.
fastest_falsification: Perturbation-sensitivity test on any published joint pipeline's outputs takes hours if checkpoints are available.

one_line: The restoration that maximizes downstream segmentation accuracy is measurably different from, and looks worse than, the restoration humans prefer.
problem: Restoration is tuned to human preference (perceptual losses, user studies) under the assumption that human-pleasing outputs are also good machine inputs.
core_hypothesis: Optimizing a restoration front-end directly for a frozen segmenter's accuracy converges to outputs with characteristic non-photorealistic signatures (exaggerated boundary contrast, suppressed texture) that humans rate as worse, revealing a systematic divergence between perceptual and task-utility optima.
falsifiable_prediction: A restoration model fine-tuned only with downstream segmentation loss will beat a perceptually tuned model on mIoU by a clear margin while losing a two-alternative human preference test on the same images.
why_important: It quantifies how much accuracy pipelines sacrifice by insisting on human-pleasing intermediates and motivates storing machine-facing and human-facing restorations separately.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: task-driven restoration exists, but a controlled quantification of the perceptual-cost-versus-utility-gain frontier with human raters appears less common; needs literature check.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one restorer with segmentation loss and one with perceptual loss from the same initialization, evaluate both on mIoU and on a small human preference study.
main_risk: The divergence may be small on mildly degraded natural images and only large under severe degradation, limiting generality of the headline claim.
default_community_belief: Perceptually better restorations are assumed to be better inputs for downstream vision models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern segmenters trained on diverse data may be near-invariant to the stylistic differences between the two optima, making the utility gap negligible.
fastest_falsification: Skip training: compare frozen-segmenter accuracy on outputs of existing distortion-oriented versus perception-oriented SR checkpoints; if no gap exists, the strong version is falsified.

one_line: Restoration-induced boundary shifts are directional (systematic erosion or dilation per structure type), not zero-mean noise, so they bias measurements rather than adding variance.
problem: When restoration changes segmentation output, the change is implicitly modeled as symmetric jitter; whether it has a consistent sign per structure polarity is untested.
core_hypothesis: Restoration priors favor smooth extended regions, so dark thin structures on bright backgrounds are systematically eroded and bright regions dilated; the induced boundary shift has a nonzero mean whose sign is predictable from local polarity and curvature.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed boundary displacement between masks computed on original versus restored images will show a nonzero mean conditioned on structure polarity, consistent in sign across restoration models sharing training distributions.
why_important: Zero-mean errors average out across measurements; directional bias corrupts every area, width, and count statistic in the same direction, which matters for longitudinal and quantitative studies that assume preprocessing is neutral.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: decomposing restoration-induced segmentation change into bias and variance components conditioned on polarity appears less explored than reporting aggregate IoU deltas.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On any dataset, compute signed distance between boundary points of masks from original and restored images, stratify by local polarity and curvature, and test the mean against zero with sign consistency across two restorers.
main_risk: Polarity-conditioned bias may vary strongly across restoration architectures, weakening the claim to a per-model property rather than a general law.
default_community_belief: Preprocessing-induced segmentation changes are treated as symmetric noise that ensembling or averaging can remove.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenter decision thresholds may already absorb small intensity shifts, leaving no measurable directional displacement at mask level.
fastest_falsification: A few hours of signed-distance analysis with existing checkpoints on one dataset.

one_line: Segmentation networks are far more robust to texture-destroying degradations than to contour-degrading ones, inverting the texture-bias narrative imported from classification.
problem: Robustness intuitions for dense prediction are borrowed from classification studies showing CNN texture bias, but segmentation supervision explicitly rewards boundary accuracy, which may reverse the dependence.
core_hypothesis: At matched information removal, degradations that scramble texture but preserve contours (texture randomization, moderate noise) cost segmentation little, while degradations that blur or displace contours at equal perceptual severity cost disproportionately, because dense training installs shape-dominant features.
falsifiable_prediction: On a degradation battery equalized by human-rated severity or mutual-information proxies, contour-corrupting transforms will produce at least twice the mIoU drop of texture-corrupting transforms for segmentation models, a ratio that will not hold for classification models on the same backbone.
why_important: Robustness engineering (augmentation menus, restoration priorities) currently inherits classification-derived rankings; if segmentation robustness is contour-dominated, restoration effort should be reallocated toward deblurring and edge preservation rather than denoising.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: task-conditional reversal of the texture-shape robustness ordering, tested with matched backbones across tasks, appears not to be an established result; needs literature search.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply matched-severity texture-only and contour-only corruptions to one benchmark, evaluate a segmentation model and a classification model sharing a backbone, and compare degradation ratios.
main_risk: Equalizing severity across corruption families is the crux; a bad severity axis makes the ratio arbitrary.
default_community_belief: Texture bias findings from classification transfer to dense prediction, so texture-corrupting degradations are treated as the primary robustness threat.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transformer-based segmenters may be texture-hungry in ways that restore the classification ordering, making the effect architecture-specific.
fastest_falsification: One-day corruption battery on published checkpoints for both tasks.

one_line: Restoration and segmentation models share the same learned natural-image prior, so their errors are correlated and cascade ensembling yields far less than independence predicts.
problem: Pipelines assume restoration errors and segmentation errors are roughly independent, so combining restored-input and raw-input predictions should average errors away; the shared-prior structure of both model families is ignored.
core_hypothesis: Because restorers and segmenters are trained on overlapping natural-image distributions, both fail on the same improbable-under-the-prior content; error overlap between segment(restore(x)) and segment(x) is therefore much higher than chance, and ensembling the two gives only marginal gains precisely on the hardest content.
falsifiable_prediction: Pixelwise error overlap between the two pipeline variants will substantially exceed the product of their marginal error rates, and oracle-ensemble upper bounds will show the smallest headroom in regions scored as improbable by an independent density model.
why_important: Redundancy planning in deployed systems (run it raw and restored, then vote) is built on the independence assumption; demonstrating prior-induced correlation changes how safety margins for degraded-input vision should be computed.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: error-correlation analysis between restoration-preprocessed and raw pipelines, tied explicitly to shared prior probability, appears less explored than model ensembling literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one degraded benchmark, compute per-pixel error sets for both pipeline variants, measure overlap against the independence baseline, and stratify headroom by density-model likelihood.
main_risk: Error overlap can also arise from shared degradation severity rather than shared priors; severity must be controlled as a covariate.
default_community_belief: Running segmentation on both raw and restored inputs provides substantially independent looks at the scene.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If segmentation errors are dominated by annotation noise or class confusion rather than prior-improbable content, overlap would be high for reasons unrelated to shared priors.
fastest_falsification: Overlap-versus-independence computation on existing predictions takes hours.

one_line: The residual uncertainty of a restoration model predicts where a downstream segmenter will fail better than the segmenter's own confidence does.
problem: Failure prediction for segmentation under degraded inputs relies on the segmenter's confidence, which is known to be unreliable; the restoration stage possesses complementary information about what was unrecoverable but it is discarded.
core_hypothesis: Regions where a restoration model's output is unstable (across seeds, timesteps, or checkpoints) mark evidence-poor image areas; these instability maps localize downstream segmentation errors better than segmenter confidence because they measure input evidence rather than decision confidence.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking pixels by restoration instability will retrieve segmentation errors with higher area under the sparsification curve than ranking by segmenter softmax confidence, on degraded inputs across at least two datasets.
why_important: It reframes failure prediction as an input-evidence problem solvable by the preprocessing stage, giving deployed pipelines an error-locator that does not require touching the segmenter.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: using restoration-stage instability as a segmentation error localizer, rather than as an image-quality diagnostic, appears less explored; not primarily a calibration contribution but an information-routing one.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate multi-seed diffusion restorations for one degraded dataset, compute per-pixel output variance, and compare error-retrieval curves against segmenter confidence baselines.
main_risk: Restoration instability and segmenter confidence may both track trivial boundary proximity, requiring distance-to-boundary matching to show any nontrivial advantage.
default_community_belief: The segmentation model itself is the natural and best source of information about where it will fail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenter confidence, for all its flaws, sees task-relevant features that restoration variance cannot, and may dominate once boundary proximity is controlled.
fastest_falsification: Sparsification-curve comparison with an off-the-shelf diffusion restorer, one day including sampling.

one_line: Downstream segmentation accuracy versus SR upscaling factor is non-monotonic, peaking below the native resolution at the onset of hallucination.
problem: Practitioners assume that super-resolving closer to native resolution is monotonically better for downstream tasks, so pipelines default to the largest available SR factor.
core_hypothesis: As SR factor increases, genuine detail recovery saturates while hallucination grows, so task utility follows an inverted-U; the peak location is predictable from the SR model's per-factor residual statistics on held-out paired data.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping SR factors (2x, 4x, 8x) on the same LR inputs will show segmentation accuracy peaking at an intermediate factor for high-degradation inputs, with the peak shifting toward higher factors as input quality improves.
why_important: A predictable utility peak turns SR-factor selection from folklore into measurement, and directly contradicts the more-resolution-is-better default baked into pipeline design.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: per-factor utility curves exist in scattered ablations, but a systematic non-monotonicity claim with a predictive rule for peak location appears untested; literature check required.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One paired dataset, one SR family with multiple factors, one frozen segmenter; plot utility versus factor at three input degradation levels.
main_risk: The non-monotonicity may only appear with generative SR models and vanish for regression-based SR, restricting the claim's scope.
default_community_belief: Super-resolving to the highest available factor before analysis is the safe default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenters may downweight fabricated high-frequency content enough that utility simply saturates rather than declines.
fastest_falsification: Factor-sweep evaluation with existing checkpoints, roughly one day.

one_line: When annotations are drawn on enhanced or restored views, models trained on raw images inherit the enhancement model's hallucinations through the labels.
problem: Annotation tooling commonly shows enhanced, denoised, or contrast-adjusted views to annotators, but the trained model consumes raw images; the label-side contamination path from restoration hallucination into ground truth is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Labels created on restored views encode boundary placements and structure completions that exist only in the restored image; models trained raw-image-to-such-labels learn to predict the restoration model's biases, effectively distilling the restorer through the annotation channel.
falsifiable_prediction: For a dataset annotated twice (on raw views and on restored views), a model trained on restored-view labels will reproduce restoration-specific structures on test images where the restorer hallucinates, at a rate significantly above a raw-label-trained model.
why_important: It identifies a contamination pathway that survives even perfectly raw training pipelines, implying dataset documentation must record the annotation viewing transform as a first-class provenance field.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotation-view provenance as a vector for restoration-bias inheritance appears undocumented in dataset audit literature; needs search.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate a small subset of one dataset on raw and enhanced views, train small models on each label set, and test for restoration-signature structures in predictions on held-out hallucination-prone images.
main_risk: Dual annotation is costly and inter-annotator variance may swamp the view effect at small scale.
default_community_belief: Ground-truth quality depends on annotator skill and protocol; the image rendering shown during annotation is treated as irrelevant.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may rely on shape priors robust to the viewing transform, so the labels would differ mainly in noise, not in systematic restoration bias.
fastest_falsification: Compare existing labels against raw versus enhanced image evidence on a dataset whose annotation protocol is documented; measurable in days without new annotation if protocol metadata exists.

one_line: Low-light enhancement style acts as a semantic class prior: the same pixels receive different class labels depending on which enhancement network prepared the image.
problem: Low-light segmentation pipelines treat enhancement as visibility correction, assuming class decisions depend on scene content rather than on the enhancement network's stylistic choices.
core_hypothesis: Enhancement networks impose learned illumination and color statistics that shift ambiguous regions across class decision boundaries; class flips between enhancement styles are systematic per class pair (e.g., road versus sidewalk) rather than random.
falsifiable_prediction: Running one frozen segmenter on outputs of three different enhancement models over the same night scenes will produce class-flip matrices that are significantly structured (repeatable class pairs) rather than uniform, and the flip structure will be predictable from each enhancer's color transfer statistics.
why_important: If preprocessing style shifts semantics, benchmark comparisons of night segmentation methods that use different enhancers conflate segmentation ability with enhancement style, and deployment behavior changes when an enhancer is updated.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: enhancement is usually evaluated by downstream accuracy; characterizing the class-flip structure it induces as a systematic prior appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three pretrained enhancers, one segmenter, one night-driving dataset; compute cross-enhancer class-flip matrices and test for structure against a permutation baseline.
main_risk: Flips may concentrate on a few genuinely ambiguous classes, making the finding real but of limited scope.
default_community_belief: Enhancement improves visibility uniformly and does not change what things are, only how visible they are.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern segmenters heavily augmented with color jitter may be invariant to enhancement style, leaving flip rates near noise level.
fastest_falsification: One-day inference-only study with existing checkpoints.

one_line: Segmentation models trained on JPEG-compressed data learn the 8x8 block grid as a boundary prior, measurably snapping mask edges to block boundaries.
problem: Most large segmentation datasets are stored as JPEG, embedding a fixed periodic artifact structure into training images; whether models internalize the block grid as a spatial prior is untested.
core_hypothesis: Block-boundary gradients act as weak but persistent edge evidence during training; trained models therefore place mask boundaries on the 8-pixel grid at above-chance rates, especially in low-contrast regions, and this bias transfers to uncompressed test images.
falsifiable_prediction: The histogram of predicted boundary positions modulo 8 will deviate from uniform for JPEG-trained models on PNG test images, with the deviation growing as local image contrast decreases, and shrinking for models trained on losslessly stored data.
why_important: A grid-locked boundary prior is a dataset-format artifact contaminating every boundary-precision claim at the 1-3 pixel scale, exactly the scale where modern methods now compete.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: JPEG effects on classification are studied; a positional mod-8 analysis of segmentation boundary placement appears not to exist; literature check needed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two public segmenters on lossless imagery, compute boundary-position histograms modulo 8 stratified by local contrast, and compare against a model trained on lossless data if available.
main_risk: Resizing and augmentation during training may destroy grid alignment, diluting the effect below detectability.
default_community_belief: Storage compression of training data is a negligible detail below the level of augmentation noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random crops during training decouple image coordinates from block phase, which may fully randomize the prior the model could learn.
fastest_falsification: Boundary phase histogram on existing predictions takes hours.

one_line: Motion deblurring collapses the exposure interval to an arbitrary instant, so segmenting deblurred frames localizes moving objects at a biased time point.
problem: Deblurring before segmentation is standard for motion-blurred footage, but a blurred object is a time integral; which instant the deblurred image represents, and hence where the object boundary is placed in time, is undefined and unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Deblurring networks systematically reconstruct an instant biased toward one end of the exposure (set by training data conventions), so segmented positions of moving objects carry a consistent temporal offset convertible into a spatial bias proportional to velocity.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic blur generated from high-fps video with known ground truth per instant, the deblurred-then-segmented object position will align with a consistent quantile of the exposure interval across scenes and speeds, not with the interval midpoint, and the spatial bias will grow linearly with object speed.
why_important: Downstream velocity estimation, collision prediction, and tracking assume deblurred frames represent exposure midpoints; a consistent temporal bias corrupts these geometrically, and it is invisible in image-quality metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: temporal semantics of deblurred outputs are discussed for extreme cases (blur-to-video), but the induced segmentation position bias as a measurable law appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize blur from high-fps clips, deblur with two pretrained models, segment, and regress recovered object position against per-instant ground truth to estimate the represented time quantile.
main_risk: Deblurring networks may be inconsistent across scenes, yielding a distribution over instants rather than a clean bias, which weakens but does not kill the claim.
default_community_belief: A deblurred frame is treated as the sharp image of the scene at that frame's timestamp.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging over training data may make networks reconstruct the exposure midpoint after all, in which case the bias is zero and only variance remains.
fastest_falsification: One-day synthetic study with existing deblurring checkpoints and high-fps public video.

one_line: Hallucinated structures in generative restoration are unstable across sampler seeds while genuinely recovered structures are stable, enabling a training-free hallucination detector.
problem: There is no accepted way to flag which parts of a diffusion-restored image are evidence-supported versus invented, blocking safe use of generative restoration in analysis pipelines.
core_hypothesis: Evidence-constrained pixels are pinned by the likelihood term and reproduce across seeds, whereas prior-driven fabrications sit in flat regions of the posterior and vary across seeds; cross-seed structural disagreement therefore localizes hallucination.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired degraded/clean data, per-pixel cross-seed variance of diffusion restorations will rank hallucinated pixels (defined by disagreement with the clean reference) with high retrieval performance, and will beat single-output image-space heuristics like local sharpness.
why_important: A reliable evidence map would let downstream segmentation consume generative restorations selectively, unlocking their quality benefits without inheriting fabrications in measurement-critical regions.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: seed-ensemble variance is used for uncertainty in generation broadly; validating it specifically as a hallucination localizer against paired ground truth in restoration appears less established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample 8 seeds from one diffusion restorer on a paired benchmark, compute cross-seed variance maps, and measure retrieval of reference-disagreement pixels against sharpness and confidence baselines.
main_risk: Consistent hallucinations (the model inventing the same structure every seed) would evade the detector precisely in the most dangerous cases; the false-negative structure must be characterized.
default_community_belief: Hallucination in restoration is treated as an unavoidable qualitative risk to be managed by choosing conservative models rather than something measurable per pixel.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong classifier-free guidance and low-temperature sampling can collapse seed diversity, making fabrications reproducible and the variance signal blind.
fastest_falsification: One-day multi-seed sampling and retrieval analysis on an existing paired benchmark.

one_line: Generative restoration fabricates objects preferentially at contextually plausible locations, so hallucination-induced false positives evade anomaly-based quality control.
problem: Quality control for restored imagery assumes fabrications look anomalous or out of place; the conditional structure of generative priors suggests the opposite.
core_hypothesis: Because diffusion priors model context-object co-occurrence, fabrications appear exactly where such objects are likely (a car on a road, a nucleus in tissue), so downstream segmentation false positives on restored images cluster in high-plausibility locations and pass contextual anomaly filters.
falsifiable_prediction: False-positive segments on restored images will score higher on context-plausibility models than false positives on raw degraded images, and anomaly detectors will catch a significantly smaller fraction of restoration-induced false positives than of noise-induced ones.
why_important: It shows that the standard safety net for restoration pipelines is structurally mismatched to the threat: the failure mode is plausible insertion, not implausible artifact, demanding evidence-based rather than plausibility-based auditing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: hallucination studies focus on frequency and fidelity; the claim that fabrications are contextually camouflaged against QC appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore degraded scenes with a generative model, collect downstream false-positive segments, score them with a context-plausibility model, and compare with false positives from matched non-generative pipelines.
main_risk: Defining and scoring context plausibility independently of the generative prior under test is delicate; a shared prior would make the result circular.
default_community_belief: Fabricated content can be caught by human review or anomaly detection because it will look subtly wrong or out of place.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration conditioned on strong evidence may fabricate mostly texture rather than objects, so object-level plausible insertions could be too rare to matter.
fastest_falsification: Count object-level insertions in an afternoon by differencing restored and reference images on a paired benchmark.

one_line: Generative restoration replaces rare structures with frequent lookalikes (mode substitution), silently collapsing rare-class recall in downstream segmentation.
problem: Restoration quality is averaged over pixels dominated by common content; what happens to rare structure categories under strong generative priors is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: When evidence is weak, diffusion restorers resolve ambiguity toward high-density modes of the training distribution, so rare classes are reconstructed as visually similar common classes; the substitution rate scales inversely with the class's prior frequency.
falsifiable_prediction: On degraded images containing rare classes, class-flip rates from rare to visually similar common classes after restoration will exceed the reverse direction by a large factor, and the asymmetry will grow with degradation severity and with guidance strength.
why_important: Rare classes are often the point of the analysis (defects, lesions, endangered species); a frequency-directed substitution bias means generative preprocessing selectively destroys the signal of interest while improving average quality metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: mode-seeking behavior is known in generative modeling; its quantification as a directional class-substitution matrix affecting downstream segmentation appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Degrade images of rare-class instances and matched common-class instances equally, restore, run a frozen segmenter, and compare directional flip rates.
main_risk: Visual similarity between class pairs must be controlled, otherwise the asymmetry could reflect classifier confusion rather than restoration substitution.
default_community_belief: Restoration errors are class-agnostic image-quality issues distributed roughly evenly over content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The likelihood term may dominate at realistic degradation levels, keeping substitutions too rare to measure outside extreme degradation.
fastest_falsification: Directional flip-rate measurement on one rare-class dataset with an off-the-shelf diffusion restorer, about a day.

one_line: No-reference image quality metrics reward hallucination: adding fabricated detail raises NR-IQA scores even when fidelity to the true scene decreases.
problem: NR-IQA scores are used to select restoration models and tune pipelines when no reference exists, assuming they proxy fidelity; generative restorers may exploit the mismatch.
core_hypothesis: NR-IQA models score naturalness and sharpness statistics, which fabrication increases; therefore among restorations at equal true fidelity, the more hallucinated one scores higher, making NR-IQA an anti-signal for evidence faithfulness precisely in the generative regime.
falsifiable_prediction: Across restoration outputs with paired references, the partial correlation between NR-IQA score and reference-fidelity will be negative once sharpness is controlled, and increasing diffusion guidance (more fabrication) will monotonically increase NR-IQA scores while decreasing per-pixel fidelity.
why_important: Model selection by NR-IQA would then systematically prefer the most hallucination-prone restorers for deployment in exactly the no-reference settings where hallucination is most dangerous for downstream segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: complaints about NR-IQA exist, but a controlled demonstration that fabrication is positively rewarded, using guidance strength as the manipulated variable, appears less established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep guidance strength on one diffusion restorer over a paired dataset, plot NR-IQA score and reference fidelity versus guidance, and test for the predicted opposite slopes.
main_risk: Some modern NR-IQA models trained on generative artifacts may already penalize fabrication, so results may split by metric generation.
default_community_belief: Higher NR-IQA scores indicate better restorations suitable for downstream use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At high guidance, artifacts may become so unnatural that NR-IQA drops, making the relation non-monotonic rather than opposite-signed.
fastest_falsification: Guidance-sweep plus metric evaluation is an afternoon with existing checkpoints.

one_line: Deterministic samplers do not reduce restoration hallucination; they make it reproducible, defeating ensemble-based detection while preserving the error.
problem: Deterministic sampling (DDIM-style, distilled one-step models) is treated as the safe choice for restoration because outputs are repeatable; whether repeatability equals faithfulness is not examined.
core_hypothesis: Determinism selects one point from the same posterior the stochastic sampler explores; fabrication mass does not shrink, it becomes invisible to seed-variance auditing, so deterministic pipelines carry equal hallucination with strictly less detectability.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched perceptual quality, deterministic and stochastic sampling of the same restorer will show equal rates of reference-disagreement structures on paired data, while cross-run variance flags a large fraction of them only in the stochastic case.
why_important: Regulated deployments are standardizing on deterministic inference for reproducibility; if reproducibility is being mistaken for reliability, audit protocols built on repeat-inference agreement are giving false assurance.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the determinism-versus-faithfulness distinction is often conflated in practice; a controlled equal-quality comparison of hallucination rates and detectability appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one restorer with deterministic and stochastic samplers on a paired benchmark, match output quality, and compare hallucination rates and the fraction detectable by repeat-run disagreement.
main_risk: Matching quality across samplers is nontrivial; unmatched comparisons would confound sampler with operating point.
default_community_belief: Deterministic inference is safer for deployment because identical inputs give identical, auditable outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deterministic trajectories may in fact concentrate on higher-likelihood solutions with genuinely fewer fabrications, making determinism mildly protective rather than neutral.
fastest_falsification: Paired-benchmark comparison with both samplers, one day including sampling time.

one_line: Generative restoration completes broken contours using amodal-completion priors, injecting false connectivity into vessel, crack, and boundary topology.
problem: Topology-sensitive applications (vasculature, cracks, road networks) increasingly use restoration preprocessing, but generative priors trained on whole objects may prefer closed, connected shapes regardless of evidence.
core_hypothesis: Diffusion restorers inherit a completion prior that bridges evidence gaps in curvilinear structures; restored images therefore show systematically higher connectivity than ground truth, and downstream segmentation inherits false merges rather than random topology noise.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired data with genuinely discontinuous structures, restored images will yield segmentations with significantly more false bridges than false breaks (an asymmetry), whereas non-generative denoising will show balanced or break-dominated topology errors.
why_important: Connectivity is the clinically and structurally meaningful quantity in these domains; a directional bias toward false merges corrupts flow modeling, severity grading, and network extraction in ways aggregate Dice never reveals.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: topology-aware segmentation is studied, but attributing a directional connectivity bias to the restoration prior, with the break/bridge asymmetry as signature, appears new; needs literature check.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired degraded/clean sets with annotated discontinuities, restore with generative and non-generative models, and compare false-bridge versus false-break rates in downstream masks.
main_risk: Segmentation models themselves carry completion priors; disentangling restorer-injected from segmenter-injected connectivity requires the non-generative control arm.
default_community_belief: Restoration errors degrade boundary precision but topology errors are treated as a segmentation-model problem, not a preprocessing problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The likelihood term at real gap locations may be strong enough (visible background through the gap) to suppress bridging in practice.
fastest_falsification: Bridge/break asymmetry count on one retinal-vessel or crack dataset with added degradation, roughly two days.

one_line: Restoration hallucination is frequency-anisotropic: fabricated fine texture is spatially well-placed while mid-frequency structure is misplaced, concentrating downstream errors at object scale.
problem: Hallucination is discussed as a single phenomenon, but which spatial scales carry the fabrication error determines whether segmentation (a mid-frequency task) is harmed.
core_hypothesis: Generative restorers synthesize locally conditioned texture accurately positioned by surrounding evidence, but commit to wrong global hypotheses under weak evidence, so reconstruction error concentrates in a mid-frequency band that overlaps the scales segmentation decisions depend on.
falsifiable_prediction: Band-pass decomposition of restoration error on paired data will show error energy peaking at object-scale frequencies rather than at the finest scales, and downstream segmentation error will correlate with mid-band error but not with fine-band error.
why_important: It explains why sharpening-based quality impressions mispredict task damage and gives a frequency-resolved audit tool: monitoring mid-band disagreement instead of full-image metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: frequency analyses of SR exist for aliasing; connecting the error spectrum to downstream segmentation damage as the operative mechanism appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute band-wise error spectra of restored images on a paired benchmark and regress downstream per-region segmentation error on band-limited error energies.
main_risk: Frequency bands and object scales overlap only loosely; a scale-matched analysis per object size class is needed to avoid smearing the effect.
default_community_belief: Hallucination is finest-detail fabrication; the coarse structure of restored images is assumed trustworthy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong conditioning may pin mid frequencies effectively, pushing fabrication entirely into fine texture where segmentation is insensitive, which would make generative restoration safer than this hypothesis claims.
fastest_falsification: Band-pass error analysis on existing paired restoration outputs, hours of compute.

one_line: SR models snap ambiguous glyph-like regions to valid-looking characters, producing confidently wrong text and markings in restored images and their segmentations.
problem: Restored imagery increasingly feeds OCR and marking-recognition pipelines (license plates, labels, signage); how SR resolves sub-legible glyph ambiguity is a safety question, not a quality question.
core_hypothesis: Trained on text-rich data, SR models learn glyph priors that act as discrete attractors: sub-legible input is pulled to the nearest valid glyph shape rather than left ambiguous, so restored text is plausible, specific, and frequently wrong, with errors that are semantic substitutions rather than blur.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetically downsampled text at sizes below legibility, SR outputs will produce clean readable glyphs whose OCR error pattern is dominated by character substitutions with high OCR confidence, unlike bicubic upsampling whose errors are rejections or low-confidence reads.
why_important: Confident substitution is the worst failure mode for evidentiary and forensic use of restored imagery; demonstrating and quantifying the attractor behavior defines where generative SR must be prohibited.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: anecdotes about text hallucination circulate, but a controlled sub-legibility substitution-versus-rejection analysis with confidence characterization appears unpublished; must verify against forensic imaging literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render text at controlled sizes, downsample below legibility, super-resolve with two generative SR models, and classify OCR outcomes into correct, substitution, and rejection with confidence.
main_risk: Results will depend strongly on SR training data text density; models never exposed to text may blur rather than snap, restricting scope to text-trained models.
default_community_belief: SR degrades gracefully on illegible content, producing blur rather than specific wrong content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Diffusion SR at low guidance may genuinely produce ambiguous glyph blends rather than committing, in which case the attractor model is wrong for that model class.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic text-size sweep with existing SR checkpoints and an OCR engine, one day.

one_line: Fabrication rate in generative restoration varies systematically with image position, inheriting the spatial composition bias of the generator's training data.
problem: Hallucination is analyzed content-wise but not position-wise; generative models are known to have spatially non-uniform priors (subjects centered, sky on top), and restoration conditioned on weak evidence may express them.
core_hypothesis: Under matched local evidence quality, the probability and semantic type of fabricated content depend on absolute position in the frame: object-like fabrications concentrate centrally, background-texture fabrications peripherally, mirroring training-composition statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: Position-stratified fabrication analysis on paired data with spatially uniform degradation will show a significant center-periphery gradient in object-insertion rates that persists after controlling for local content, and the gradient will track the generator's training-set composition statistics.
why_important: Position-dependent hallucination invalidates spatially uniform trust in restored images; croppings and tilings of the same scene would carry different fabrication risk, which matters for tiled processing of large images.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: spatial biases of generation are documented for synthesis; carrying the analysis into restoration conditioned on real evidence appears not yet done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply uniform degradation to a paired dataset, restore, detect fabricated segments by reference comparison, and fit fabrication rate as a function of normalized image coordinates with content controls.
main_risk: Real scene composition is itself position-biased, so content controls must be strong; synthetic scenes with randomized layouts may be needed for a clean test.
default_community_belief: Fabrication risk is a function of local evidence quality and content, not of where a pixel sits in the frame.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Convolutional restorers with limited receptive fields may lack access to absolute position, muting any positional prior except near borders.
fastest_falsification: Position-stratified insertion counting on tiled versus centered crops of identical content, about a day.

one_line: Super-resolution amplifies adversarial perturbations: imperceptible LR-space attacks can steer restored content and flip downstream segmentation at will.
problem: Adding SR preprocessing changes the downstream model's attack surface, but robustness evaluations treat the pipeline as if the segmenter alone defines vulnerability.
core_hypothesis: Because SR inverts a many-to-one degradation, small LR perturbations select among divergent HR reconstructions; attack energy is amplified by the generator's Jacobian in hallucination-prone regions, making segment(SR(x)) strictly easier to attack than segment(upsample(x)) at matched perturbation budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Under equal LR-space epsilon budgets, targeted mask-flipping attacks will succeed at substantially higher rates through the SR pipeline than through bicubic upsampling, with success concentrated where cross-seed SR variance is high.
why_important: Pipelines add SR expecting benign quality gains; showing it functions as an adversarial amplifier reframes preprocessing choices as security decisions and links attack surface to measurable hallucination propensity.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: attacks on SR outputs exist as image-quality attacks; quantifying SR as a downstream-task attack amplifier with a hallucination-locality prediction appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched-budget PGD attacks against both pipelines on one dataset, compare success rates, and correlate per-region success with cross-seed SR variance maps.
main_risk: Gradient masking through the SR model can distort attack comparisons; gradient-free or transfer attacks are needed as controls.
default_community_belief: Preprocessing modules are security-neutral; adversarial robustness is a property of the recognition model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SR nonlinearity might instead destroy adversarial structure like a defense-by-transformation, making the pipeline harder to attack, which would itself be a useful negative result.
fastest_falsification: Matched-budget attack comparison with existing checkpoints, two days including attack tuning.

one_line: The internal features of a generative restorer identify which output pixels it invented, better than any image-space detector applied to its output.
problem: Hallucination detection is attempted post hoc on the restored image, discarding the generator's internal computation that produced the fabrication.
core_hypothesis: During generation the model resolves an evidence-versus-prior competition per region; this resolution is linearly decodable from intermediate activations, so a lightweight probe on generator internals will localize fabricated pixels with higher accuracy than external detectors that only see the output image.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear or shallow probe trained on generator activations will exceed image-space hallucination detectors (sharpness, artifact classifiers, cross-seed variance from fewer seeds) at fabricated-pixel retrieval on held-out paired data, and the advantage will survive transfer to unseen degradation types.
why_important: It would give single-pass, deployment-cheap evidence maps for generative restoration, and scientifically it tests whether fabrication is represented as an explicit internal state rather than an emergent output property.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: probing internals for truthfulness is active in language models; a systematic evidence-versus-prior probe for restoration diffusion internals appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On paired data, label fabricated pixels by reference disagreement, train a probe on mid-network activations of the restorer, and compare retrieval against external baselines with matched supervision.
main_risk: The probe may learn degradation-severity correlates rather than fabrication per se; transfer tests across degradation types are the necessary control.
default_community_belief: Hallucination must be caught from outputs because generation internals are treated as uninterpretable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fabrication may be distributed across timesteps and layers with no compact readout, making probes no better than output statistics.
fastest_falsification: Probe training on cached activations for one restorer and one paired dataset, about two days.

one_line: Chained restoration operations compound fabrication superlinearly, and pipeline order changes what gets invented more than parameter settings do.
problem: Practical pipelines chain denoising, deblurring, and SR, but hallucination is only ever measured for single models; interaction effects across stages are unknown.
core_hypothesis: Each stage treats the previous stage's fabrications as evidence, so fabrication accumulates multiplicatively along the chain; consequently total invented content grows faster than the sum of single-stage rates, and reordering stages changes fabrication content more than tuning any single stage's strength.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired data, fabricated-pixel area for denoise-deblur-SR chains will exceed the sum of individual-stage fabrications at matched final quality, and permuting stage order will change fabricated-content overlap (measured by IoU of fabrication masks) more than a wide sweep of per-stage strength parameters.
why_important: Deployment pipelines are assembled stage-by-stage with per-stage validation; superlinear compounding means stage-level audits certify nothing about the pipeline, requiring end-to-end fabrication accounting.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: restoration-pipeline interaction effects on hallucination appear unstudied; individual-model hallucination work does not compose obviously.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Factorial experiment over stage order and strengths on one paired benchmark, measuring fabrication masks per configuration against reference.
main_risk: Matched-final-quality comparison across orders is hard to achieve; without it, order effects confound with operating point.
default_community_belief: A pipeline of individually validated restoration stages is as trustworthy as its weakest stage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Later stages may actually suppress earlier fabrications by treating them as artifacts, making compounding sublinear in some orders, which would still be a valuable ordering law.
fastest_falsification: Two-stage (denoise then SR versus SR then denoise) fabrication comparison on one dataset, one day.

one_line: The synthetic-to-real robustness gap in degraded-image segmentation is largely noise-model mis-specification with a predictable failure direction, not an amorphous domain gap.
problem: Robustness training uses Gaussian noise and bicubic blur, then failures on real sensor data are attributed to a generic domain gap without asking which physical mismatch caused them.
core_hypothesis: Real low-light noise is signal-dependent (Poisson-dominated) and spatially correlated after ISP processing; models hardened on white Gaussian noise therefore fail specifically in dark signal-dependent-variance regions, and the error map is predictable from the local divergence between assumed and actual noise models.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-region segmentation degradation on real low-light data will correlate with a computable noise-model divergence map (Gaussian assumption versus estimated Poisson-Gaussian parameters), and retraining with the corrected noise model will remove most of the gap without any other domain adaptation.
why_important: It converts robustness from empirical augmentation search into physics-informed model checking: if failure direction is predictable from noise-model divergence, robustness budgets can be allocated analytically.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: physics-based noise modeling exists in denoising literature; using noise-model divergence as a quantitative predictor of segmentation failure geography appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate Poisson-Gaussian parameters on a real low-light segmentation set, compute divergence maps against the training-time noise assumption, and regress per-region accuracy drop on divergence; then retrain with corrected noise synthesis.
main_risk: ISP-induced spatial correlation may dominate over the Poisson mismatch, requiring the analysis to model both terms to avoid mis-attribution.
default_community_belief: Synthetic-corruption robustness generalizes to real degradations up to a residual domain gap that only more real data can close.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failures might be dominated by content shifts co-occurring with low light (different scenes at night) rather than by noise statistics, which the divergence map would not capture.
fastest_falsification: Correlation between divergence maps and error maps on one real low-light dataset requires no training, one day.

one_line: The camera ISP is a hidden confounder in segmentation datasets: much of what is called cross-camera domain shift is reproducible ISP shift.
problem: Cross-device generalization failures are attributed to optics, sensors, and scene statistics; the deterministic and vendor-specific ISP transform sitting between sensor and dataset is rarely isolated.
core_hypothesis: Rendering the same raw captures through different ISP pipelines changes segmentation outputs substantially; a large fraction of measured cross-camera accuracy drop can be reproduced by ISP substitution alone, holding sensor and scene fixed.
falsifiable_prediction: Using raw-capable datasets, the accuracy drop from evaluating a model on camera B instead of camera A will be reproduced to a large fraction by evaluating on camera A raws re-rendered with camera B's ISP emulation, and ISP-augmented training will recover most of the cross-camera gap.
why_important: If ISP explains much of device shift, domain adaptation research is partly solving the wrong problem, and dataset builders could publish raw or ISP-documented data to eliminate a major generalization confounder cheaply.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: ISP effects are studied for photography and detection robustness in places; a decomposition of segmentation domain shift into ISP versus residual components appears not standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one raw image set, render through three ISP emulations, measure cross-render segmentation consistency of a frozen model, and compare against reported cross-camera gaps.
main_risk: Faithful ISP emulation is hard; a weak emulator underestimates the ISP share of the gap.
default_community_belief: Cross-camera degradation reflects sensor and scene differences that require learned domain adaptation to bridge.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models trained on web-scale ISP diversity may already be ISP-invariant, leaving optics and scene content as the true drivers.
fastest_falsification: Cross-render consistency measurement with an open ISP emulator on one raw dataset, one day.

one_line: Segmentation models exploit demosaicing correlations as features, so RAW-trained and RGB-trained models generalize differently under resampling and novel sensors.
problem: Every RGB training image carries demosaicing-induced inter-channel correlations from the Bayer pattern; whether dense predictors depend on these micro-correlations is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Models learn to use demosaicing correlation patterns as a weak texture prior; operations that destroy them (resampling, novel color filter arrays, synthetic rendering) remove a feature the model silently depends on, explaining part of the synthetic-to-real and cross-sensor gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating demosaicing correlations at test time (channel-decorrelating micro-shuffles that preserve appearance) will degrade RGB-trained segmenters measurably more than RAW-trained or heavily resampled-trained counterparts, and the degradation will exceed human-perceptible image change.
why_important: A dependence on invisible pipeline artifacts would mean reported robustness numbers are entangled with capture-pipeline consistency, and synthetic data will underperform for reasons unrelated to content realism.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: demosaicing forensics is established; its role as a learned feature in dense prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design an appearance-preserving decorrelation perturbation, verify imperceptibility, and measure segmentation degradation for models trained on RGB versus resample-augmented data.
main_risk: Constructing a perturbation that removes demosaicing correlation without touching any other cue is technically delicate; leakage would confound the ablation.
default_community_belief: Models learn from image content; invisible capture-pipeline correlations are beneath the level features respond to.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggressive training-time augmentation (resizing, compression) may already destroy demosaicing correlations, so trained models never learned to use them.
fastest_falsification: Micro-perturbation ablation on public checkpoints, roughly two days including perturbation validation.

one_line: Photon noise is informative, not just corruptive: noise variance encodes luminance, and segmentation networks measurably use it, which denoising removes.
problem: Denoising is framed as removing a nuisance, but in signal-dependent noise regimes the local noise level itself carries scene information that networks could exploit.
core_hypothesis: Under Poisson-dominated noise, local variance is a luminance channel; segmenters trained on noisy data learn to read it, so denoised inputs deprive them of a used cue and matched-training comparisons will show noisy-input models beating denoised-input models in shadow regions.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained and tested on noisy low-light images will outperform models trained and tested on denoised versions of the same images specifically in low-luminance regions, and variance-scrambling perturbations that preserve mean appearance will selectively hurt the noisy-trained model.
why_important: It challenges the universal denoise-first doctrine with an information-theoretic account: preprocessing that maximizes visual quality can strictly reduce the information available to the task model.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: noise-as-signal is known in physics-based vision niches; a direct demonstration that dense predictors exploit noise variance as a feature appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Matched training runs on noisy versus denoised low-light data, luminance-stratified evaluation, plus the variance-scrambling probe on the noisy-trained model.
main_risk: Gains in shadows could come from denoising artifacts harming the denoised arm rather than from noise information helping the noisy arm; the scrambling probe is the disambiguating control.
default_community_belief: Noise carries no task information and its removal is always neutral-to-positive for downstream models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may be unable to estimate local variance reliably at realistic photon counts, making the available information practically unusable.
fastest_falsification: The variance-scrambling probe on an existing low-light-trained model, one day.

one_line: Segmentation accuracy under increasing degradation collapses in class-specific phase transitions predictable from each class's spatial-frequency signature.
problem: Robustness curves are reported as smooth dataset-level averages, hiding whether individual classes fail gradually or catastrophically at critical severities.
core_hypothesis: Each class depends on a characteristic spatial-frequency band for discrimination; when degradation attenuates that band below the noise floor, class accuracy collapses sharply, so per-class robustness curves are sigmoidal with transition points computable from class frequency signatures and the degradation's transfer function.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class accuracy versus blur radius or noise sigma will show sharp transitions whose ordering across classes is predicted by pre-computed class discriminability spectra, with rank correlation significantly above chance across two datasets and two architectures.
why_important: Predictable per-class collapse thresholds would enable analytic safety envelopes (which classes are trustworthy at a given measured image quality) instead of exhaustive empirical stress testing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: severity-accuracy curves are standard; deriving and validating class-wise transition points from frequency analysis appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute class discriminability spectra on clean data, predict collapse ordering, then run severity sweeps and compare observed transition points against predictions.
main_risk: Context effects (classes recognized from surroundings) can rescue classes past their own frequency collapse, blurring transitions for context-rich classes.
default_community_belief: Degradation causes gradual, roughly uniform accuracy decay that summary robustness scores capture adequately.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep features may mix frequencies enough that no clean per-class band exists, making transitions soft and prediction weak.
fastest_falsification: Severity sweep with per-class curves on one dataset and existing checkpoints, one day.

one_line: Robust segmentation networks implicitly perform blind blur-kernel estimation: the point-spread function is decodable from their features, explaining and bounding their deblurring-free robustness.
problem: Blur-robust segmenters work without explicit deblurring, but the mechanism is unexplained: do they learn blur-invariant features or blur-aware ones?
core_hypothesis: Robustness to blur is achieved by internal kernel estimation followed by kernel-conditioned interpretation; therefore the blur kernel is linearly decodable from intermediate features of blur-robust models, and robustness fails exactly for kernel families the internal estimator cannot represent.
falsifiable_prediction: Probes on blur-augmented models will recover kernel parameters substantially above chance while probes on clean-trained models will not, and generalization to held-out kernel families will be predicted by internal kernel-estimation error rather than by kernel visual similarity.
why_important: Distinguishing invariance from awareness changes how robustness should be trained and audited: kernel-aware models can be extended by broadening estimator coverage, and their failure modes are forecastable from estimator error.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: probing for nuisance parameters in robust models exists in pieces; a kernel-decodability account of blur robustness with failure prediction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train linear probes for kernel parameters on features of blur-augmented and clean segmenters, then test whether probe error on novel kernels predicts segmentation degradation.
main_risk: Kernel decodability may be a byproduct rather than a mechanism; a causal intervention (feature-space kernel-information removal) is needed to close the loop.
default_community_belief: Augmentation-trained robustness comes from learning invariant features that discard nuisance parameters like blur.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both invariance and awareness may coexist across layers, making the dichotomy too coarse to test cleanly.
fastest_falsification: Kernel-parameter probing on public robust checkpoints, one to two days.

one_line: Real-world degradations are correlated with semantics (blur on movers, defocus on background), so training with spatially uniform synthetic degradation teaches wrong invariances and can reduce real-world robustness.
problem: Synthetic corruption pipelines apply degradations independently of content, but physical degradations are caused by scene properties, creating systematic degradation-semantics correlations that uniform augmentation breaks.
core_hypothesis: Networks can exploit degradation-semantics correlations as cues (motion blur implies mover); uniform-degradation training destroys this cue and teaches an invariance that misfires on real data, so semantically correlated augmentation will beat uniform augmentation on real degraded benchmarks at matched severity distributions.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with physically plausible correlated degradation will outperform uniform-degradation counterparts on real degraded data, while performing equally or worse on uniformly corrupted synthetic tests, demonstrating the two robustness measures dissociate.
why_important: It would show that the standard synthetic robustness benchmarks select for the wrong invariances, explaining synthetic-real robustness rank inversions and redirecting augmentation design toward degradation causality.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: motion-blur-as-cue exists in video analysis; the general claim that uniform corruption training is harmful because it breaks degradation-semantics correlation appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build correlated and uniform degradation augmentation with matched marginal severity, train paired models, and evaluate on both real degraded data and uniform synthetic corruption suites.
main_risk: Constructing physically plausible correlated degradation requires scene understanding (depth, motion), and errors there would contaminate the comparison.
default_community_belief: Degradation robustness is about severity coverage; where degradation falls in the image is treated as irrelevant randomness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The correlation cue may be too weak relative to appearance cues for networks to exploit, making the two augmentation schemes equivalent in practice.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate an existing uniformly-augmented robust model on real motion-blurred data stratified by blur-semantics consistency; inconsistent regions failing worse supports the cue account, hours of analysis.

one_line: The anti-aliasing kernel used when datasets are resized is an unreported hyperparameter that measurably re-ranks segmentation methods on public benchmarks.
problem: Benchmark images pass through resize operations with library-dependent kernels (bilinear, bicubic, antialiased or not), yet papers never report them and comparisons assume the choice is neutral.
core_hypothesis: Resize-kernel choice shifts the effective frequency content of both training and test data enough to change method rankings at the margins typical of leaderboard competition (fractions of an mIoU point), so some published ordering differences are resize artifacts.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating a set of public segmentation checkpoints on the same benchmark rendered through four common resize implementations will change at least some adjacent leaderboard orderings, with boundary-heavy metrics affected more than region metrics.
why_important: If infrastructure defaults influence rankings at competitive margins, the community's incremental-progress signal is noisier than assumed and benchmark protocols need to pin resize semantics explicitly.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: resize inconsistencies are known folklore for metric reproduction; a systematic re-ranking study for segmentation benchmarks appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a benchmark and a set of checkpoints, regenerate evaluation data via four resize implementations, and quantify ranking stability with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Effects may be real but smaller than seed variance, in which case the correct conclusion is that leaderboard margins below combined seed-plus-resize noise are meaningless, still a publishable calibration of the field's noise floor.
default_community_belief: Image resizing is a solved, neutral preprocessing step with no bearing on method comparisons.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern training pipelines randomize scales heavily, which may confer enough resize invariance that rankings are stable to kernel choice.
fastest_falsification: Four-way resize re-evaluation of public checkpoints on one benchmark, one day of compute.

one_line: Dehazing systematically relocates the boundary between distant objects and sky or background, acting as a learned horizon prior rather than a neutral contrast restorer.
problem: Atmospheric scattering removes contrast at distance; dehazing models must decide where faded objects end and background begins, but this decision embeds a prior that is never audited.
core_hypothesis: Dehazing networks resolve the distance-fade ambiguity with dataset-specific priors about skyline shape and object extent, so dehazed images shift far-field segmentation boundaries in a consistent direction (extending or truncating distant structures) compared to physically corrected references.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic haze with known transmission maps, boundaries of distant objects in dehazed-then-segmented outputs will show a signed displacement relative to ground truth that is consistent across scenes for a given dehazing model but differs between models trained on different data.
why_important: Far-field boundaries feed mapping, navigation, and range-estimation stacks; a model-specific directional bias at distance is a silent geometric error source introduced by preprocessing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: dehazing evaluation focuses on image quality; a signed far-field boundary displacement analysis appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render synthetic haze over scenes with ground-truth geometry, dehaze with two models, segment with a frozen model, and measure signed distant-boundary displacement.
main_risk: Synthetic haze realism limits external validity; a real-smog paired subset would be needed for confirmation.
default_community_belief: Dehazing restores lost contrast and thereby recovers, rather than reinterprets, distant scene structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where transmission is estimated well, physics constrains the solution tightly enough that prior-driven displacement may be negligible except in extreme haze.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic-haze displacement measurement with public dehazing checkpoints, one day.

one_line: Sensor fixed-pattern noise acts as a device watermark that segmentation models learn, coupling predictions to the capture device rather than the scene.
problem: Datasets are collected with few physical cameras; each contributes a stable fixed-pattern noise fingerprint that forensics can read, and that networks may read too, creating device-label shortcuts.
core_hypothesis: When device identity correlates with label statistics in training data (different cameras used at different sites or for different classes), models exploit fixed-pattern fingerprints as features; removing or swapping fingerprints at test time will shift predictions measurably without any visible image change.
falsifiable_prediction: Fingerprint-swap perturbations (imperceptible, forensics-validated) will change class posteriors and mask outputs of models trained on multi-device datasets significantly more than random perturbations of equal energy, with the effect scaling with the training-time device-label correlation.
why_important: Device shortcuts are a contamination class invisible to content-level dataset audits and would explain cross-site failures in medical and industrial deployments beyond appearance shift.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: sensor fingerprints are standard in forensics; their exploitation by dense predictors as label shortcuts appears undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate fingerprints from a multi-device dataset, construct swap perturbations, and measure prediction shifts of a trained segmenter versus energy-matched random noise.
main_risk: Training augmentation may destroy fingerprint accessibility; a positive result likely requires datasets with light augmentation, which bounds the scope of the threat.
default_community_belief: Sub-perceptual sensor patterns are irrelevant to semantic models and only matter for forensics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fixed-pattern noise energy may simply be too small relative to shot noise for practical exploitation by networks.
fastest_falsification: Fingerprint-swap sensitivity test on one multi-device dataset and checkpoint, two days including fingerprint estimation.

one_line: Eight-bit export of high-bit-depth scientific images destroys sub-quantization gradients that annotators saw in windowed views, creating a systematic train-label mismatch.
