problem: Annotation is performed on interactively windowed high-bit-depth data (medical, microscopy), but training pipelines commonly consume 8-bit exports; the information annotators used may be absent from what models see.
core_hypothesis: Boundary placements in ground truth encode sub-8-bit intensity distinctions visible only under windowing; models trained on 8-bit data face irreducible error at these boundaries, misdiagnosed as model deficiency, and bit-depth-preserving training will disproportionately improve exactly the boundary segments where quantization removed the annotators' evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: Boundary error of 8-bit-trained models will concentrate where local dynamic range falls within one 8-bit quantization step of the full-depth data, and 16-bit training will reduce error in those regions while leaving other regions unchanged.
why_important: It reframes part of the boundary-accuracy ceiling as a data-pipeline artifact with a trivial fix, and warns that benchmark ceilings computed on 8-bit exports underestimate achievable accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: bit-depth effects are discussed for radiology viewing; a quantization-conditioned boundary-error analysis for segmentation training appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one 16-bit dataset, train matched models on 8-bit and 16-bit inputs, stratify boundary error by local sub-quantization contrast, and test for the predicted selective improvement.
main_risk: Modern normalization pipelines sometimes preserve effective dynamic range despite 8-bit storage; the analysis must verify actual information loss per dataset.
default_community_belief: Eight-bit conversion is visually lossless and therefore training-neutral for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may rely on shape priors rather than faint gradients at the disputed boundaries, in which case the mismatch is illusory.
fastest_falsification: Quantization-conditioned error stratification on an existing 16-bit dataset and 8-bit-trained model, hours.

one_line: Global exposure and gamma changes act on segmentation like class-prior shifts, changing per-class recall in lawful, predictable directions rather than adding uniform noise.
problem: Brightness variations are treated as a nuisance handled by augmentation, but their residual effect on trained models is never characterized as a structured response.
core_hypothesis: Because class appearance statistics occupy different luminance ranges, a global gamma shift moves each class's evidence distribution relative to learned decision boundaries in a class-specific direction, producing a reproducible recall-versus-gamma response curve per class, analogous to a prior shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class recall as a function of applied gamma will follow smooth, monotonic-in-opposite-directions curves for dark-associated versus bright-associated classes, reproducible across architectures trained on the same data, allowing recall change to be forecast from a class-luminance profile.
why_important: A lawful response enables analytic correction (recalibrating decision thresholds from measured scene exposure) instead of retraining, and provides a cheap audit of which classes a deployment loses at dawn and dusk.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: illumination robustness is studied via augmentation coverage; a quantitative per-class gamma-response law appears uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep gamma on a validation set, record per-class recall curves for two architectures, and test predictability from class-luminance profiles computed on training data.
main_risk: Heavy photometric augmentation during training may flatten the curves, making the law real only for lightly augmented models.
default_community_belief: Photometric augmentation makes models effectively exposure-invariant, so residual brightness effects are unstructured noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Normalization layers may absorb global gamma almost completely, leaving effects too small to form measurable curves.
fastest_falsification: Gamma-sweep evaluation on existing checkpoints, hours of compute.

one_line: Diffusion-model features encode boundary ownership (which object an edge belongs to) more explicitly than discriminative pretraining features.
problem: Edges are easy but assigning them to the correct object (occluder versus occluded) is the hard part of segmentation; which pretraining objectives produce ownership-aware features is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Generative training forces amodal reasoning about which surface produces which appearance, so diffusion U-Net features linearly encode border-ownership direction, whereas contrastive and classification features encode edge presence but not ownership.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes for border-ownership direction on occlusion-annotated datasets will score substantially higher on diffusion features than on classification, contrastive, and self-supervised-ViT features at matched feature dimensionality and probe capacity.
why_important: Border ownership is the primitive behind amodal completion, occlusion handling, and instance separation; identifying which pretraining installs it would give a principled basis for choosing segmentation backbones beyond benchmark chasing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: diffusion features are known to transfer well to segmentation; decomposing the advantage into ownership encoding specifically, with occlusion-annotated probing, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract features from four pretraining families on an occlusion-ordering dataset, train linear ownership probes, and compare accuracy under matched conditions.
main_risk: Probe results depend on layer and timestep selection for diffusion models; a fair search protocol across all families is essential to avoid tuning bias.
default_community_belief: Feature quality for segmentation is a scalar transferability property; pretraining objectives differ in amount, not kind, of spatial information.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ownership may be computed late in task decoders everywhere, with no pretraining family encoding it explicitly in features.
fastest_falsification: Linear probing study on cached features, two days including extraction.

one_line: The best diffusion timestep for segmentation features depends on object size, so any single-timestep feature extraction is provably suboptimal.
problem: Diffusion-feature pipelines pick one noise timestep by validation, implicitly assuming a globally optimal operating point exists.
core_hypothesis: Noise level acts as a spatial-frequency filter on what the denoiser must attend to: small objects are only resolvable in features at low timesteps while large-object semantics stabilize at high timesteps, so per-size optimal timesteps differ systematically and a size-adaptive readout dominates any fixed choice.
falsifiable_prediction: Segmentation accuracy per object-size bin as a function of extraction timestep will show peak locations that shift monotonically with size, and an oracle per-size timestep selector will beat the best single timestep by a margin exceeding seed variance.
why_important: It converts timestep selection from a hyperparameter into a measurable scale-analysis, predicts systematic small-object weakness of current diffusion-feature methods, and motivates multi-timestep architectures with a principled justification.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: multi-timestep fusion is used empirically; a quantified size-timestep law with oracle-gap measurement appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep timesteps on one dataset, evaluate per size bin, plot peak-timestep versus size, and compute the oracle-selector gap.
main_risk: Timestep effects may interact with layer choice, requiring a two-dimensional sweep to avoid mistaking layer artifacts for size laws.
default_community_belief: A well-chosen middle timestep provides near-optimal features for all content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: U-Net skip connections may preserve fine detail across timesteps, flattening the size dependence.
fastest_falsification: Timestep-by-size accuracy grid on one dataset, one day.

one_line: The geometry of the learned score field performs zero-shot segmentation: at moderate noise, score vectors point from boundaries toward region interiors.
problem: Diffusion models are used for segmentation via features or generation, but the score function itself is a vector field with spatial structure that has not been examined as a direct segmentation signal.
core_hypothesis: Because the score points toward higher data density and object interiors are more constrained than boundary configurations, the divergence and flow structure of the score field at intermediate noise levels aligns with region structure, so watershed-style integration of the score field yields object segments without any training.
falsifiable_prediction: Segmenting by integrating score-field flow on noised real images will substantially beat classical gradient-based watershed and be competitive with self-supervised segmentation baselines on at least simple-object datasets, with performance peaking at a characteristic noise band.
why_important: It would establish a direct mathematical link between learned data density and image partition structure, giving generative models a segmentation interpretation that is analytic rather than representational.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: score-based editing and guidance are studied; using score-field flow geometry as a standalone segmentation mechanism appears unexplored, pending literature search.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute score fields for noised images with a pretrained model, integrate flow to fixed points, cluster basins, and evaluate against unsupervised segmentation baselines.
main_risk: Score estimates in high dimensions may be too anisotropic across channels to define a usable spatial flow, requiring a projection step whose design could dominate results.
default_community_belief: Diffusion models help segmentation only through learned representations or generated samples, not through the analytic structure of the score itself.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The score at image scale mostly encodes local texture statistics; region-level structure may only exist in feature space, not in the raw field.
fastest_falsification: Basin-clustering demo on a toy dataset with a small pretrained diffusion model, two days.

one_line: Pixels that are unstable under diffusion inversion and regeneration mark object boundaries, giving an unsupervised boundary detector from any pretrained diffusion model.
problem: Unsupervised boundary discovery relies on color and texture gradients; whether generative reconstruction instability provides an independent, semantics-aware boundary signal is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Inverting an image into diffusion latent space and regenerating perturbs each pixel by an amount reflecting posterior flatness; boundaries are less constrained than interiors under the generative prior, so instability maps peak at semantic boundaries including contrast-free ones where classical gradients fail.
falsifiable_prediction: Inversion-regeneration instability maps will predict human-annotated boundaries with higher accuracy than gradient baselines specifically on low-contrast semantic boundaries, while performing comparably elsewhere.
why_important: A boundary signal that does not require intensity contrast would help exactly where current unsupervised methods fail (camouflage, illumination boundaries versus object boundaries), and would reveal what boundary knowledge generative pretraining contains.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: inversion stability is studied for editing fidelity; its use as a boundary detector with low-contrast stratified evaluation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute multi-run inversion-regeneration residuals on a boundary benchmark, stratify evaluation by local contrast, and compare against gradient and self-supervised baselines.
main_risk: Inversion error concentrates on fine texture too; separating texture instability from boundary instability may need band-pass filtering that weakens the claim's purity.
default_community_belief: Unsupervised boundary detection is limited by the information in local image gradients unless supervised semantics are added.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instability may track generation difficulty (texture complexity) more than semantic boundaries, making the map an entropy detector rather than a boundary detector.
fastest_falsification: Instability-map computation on one boundary benchmark with a public diffusion model, one day.

one_line: Cross-attention maps in text-to-image diffusion systematically under-segment objects, attending to discriminative parts, with the deficit growing with object articulation.
problem: Attention-based zero-shot segmentation extracts object masks from text-to-image cross-attention, assuming attention covers object extent; the part-versus-whole structure of that attention is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Cross-attention aligns tokens with the image evidence that disambiguates them, which is discriminative parts (heads, wheels, handles) rather than full extents, so attention-derived masks have a lawful negative bias in coverage that scales with how part-decomposable the object is.
falsifiable_prediction: Coverage ratio (attention mask area over true mask area) will be significantly below one on average, decrease with an articulation score computed from part-annotation datasets, and be lowest for classes whose discrimination depends on small parts.
why_important: Attention-derived pseudo-labels are increasingly used to train open-vocabulary segmenters; a systematic part bias would propagate into trained models as a coverage deficit that no amount of pseudo-label volume fixes.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: attention-mask quality is reported in aggregate; an articulation-conditioned coverage law and its propagation into distilled students appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract cross-attention masks for classes with part annotations, regress coverage ratio on articulation metrics, and verify the deficit transfers to a student trained on these pseudo-labels.
main_risk: Attention post-processing choices (thresholds, layer averaging) strongly affect coverage; conclusions must be shown robust across the post-processing space.
default_community_belief: Cross-attention localizes objects; errors are noise to be cleaned by refinement rather than a directional bias.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Self-attention aggregation steps used in modern extractors may already restore full extents, leaving no residual articulation-dependent bias.
fastest_falsification: Coverage-versus-articulation regression on one part-annotated dataset, one day.

one_line: Generative (diffusion-likelihood) and discriminative segmentation errors overlap precisely on ambiguous boundary pixels, so their combination fails where combination is most needed.
problem: Generative classifiers via diffusion are promoted as complementary to discriminative models, implying error diversity; where in the image the errors actually differ is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: The two paradigms err differently on interior pixels (texture confusions versus prior confusions) but identically on genuinely ambiguous boundary pixels where the information is absent from the image, so ensemble gains concentrate in already-easy regions and vanish at boundaries.
falsifiable_prediction: Pixelwise error-overlap analysis will show near-independent errors in interiors but strongly correlated errors within a fixed distance of boundaries, and ensembling will improve interior metrics while leaving boundary F-scores statistically unchanged.
why_important: It sets a fundamental limit on what paradigm diversity can buy for segmentation and redirects effort from ensembling toward changing the information available at boundaries (multi-view, priors from annotation protocols).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: generative-discriminative complementarity is asserted from aggregate metrics; a spatially resolved error-overlap decomposition appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a diffusion-based segmentation approach and a discriminative model on one benchmark, compute distance-to-boundary-stratified error correlation, and measure ensemble gains per stratum.
main_risk: Boundary annotation noise inflates apparent boundary error correlation for any model pair; a multi-annotator subset is needed to calibrate the floor.
default_community_belief: Generative and discriminative segmenters fail differently, so combining them is a promising route to robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generative models may genuinely resolve some boundary ambiguity via shape priors, producing usable boundary-zone diversity that this hypothesis denies.
fastest_falsification: Stratified error-overlap analysis on existing predictions from both paradigms, hours.

one_line: Diffusion features sweep from texture-dominant to shape-dominant along the noise axis, and a model's transfer quality to a segmentation domain is predictable from where that domain needs to sit on the spectrum.
problem: Shape-versus-texture bias is treated as a fixed property of a pretrained network, but diffusion models expose a continuum of feature regimes indexed by timestep that has not been characterized as a bias spectrum.
core_hypothesis: Cue-conflict analysis applied per timestep will reveal a monotonic texture-to-shape transition; domains whose discrimination is shape-based (silhouettes, medical organs) transfer best from high-timestep features while texture-based domains (materials, terrain) prefer low timesteps, making transfer performance forecastable from a domain's cue profile.
falsifiable_prediction: The timestep maximizing transfer accuracy per domain will correlate strongly with the domain's independently measured shape-versus-texture discriminability profile across at least five domains.
why_important: A controllable bias axis would let practitioners match features to domains analytically instead of by grid search, and gives the shape-texture literature a continuous experimental handle instead of comparing discrete architectures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: cue-conflict methodology exists for classifiers; applying it along the diffusion noise axis and validating a transfer-prediction rule appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run cue-conflict probes per timestep on one diffusion model, compute domain cue profiles for five segmentation datasets, and test the predicted correlation between profile and optimal timestep.
main_risk: Cue-conflict stimuli designed for classification may not translate cleanly to dense features, requiring new stimulus design whose validity must be established first.
default_community_belief: A pretrained network has one characteristic shape-texture bias that transfer inherits.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The spectrum may exist but be too narrow to matter, with layer choice dominating timestep choice for bias control.
fastest_falsification: Per-timestep cue-conflict measurement on one model, two days including stimulus adaptation.

one_line: Fine-tuning diffusion models for generation quality destroys their segmentation-relevant features faster than generation metrics degrade, decoupling the two capabilities.
problem: Diffusion backbones are fine-tuned (style, personalization, distillation) with generation-quality monitoring only, assuming representation quality follows generation quality.
core_hypothesis: Dense-prediction utility lives in intermediate features that fine-tuning reallocates early and silently, while output quality is preserved by later layers; therefore segmentation-probe accuracy drops steeply under fine-tuning regimes that leave FID nearly unchanged.
falsifiable_prediction: Across fine-tuning trajectories (style adaptation, step distillation), segmentation-probe accuracy on frozen features will decline several times faster in relative terms than FID or human-rated generation quality, with step-distilled models showing the largest representational loss.
why_important: The community increasingly consumes distilled and adapted diffusion models as feature extractors; if representation decays invisibly, feature-based pipelines inherit silent regressions, and checkpoints need representation scorecards alongside generation metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: representation quality of diffusion models is studied for base checkpoints; its dynamics under generation-targeted fine-tuning appear uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one base model, apply three fine-tuning regimes with checkpoints along each trajectory, and track probe-based segmentation accuracy against generation metrics.
main_risk: Probe-based measurement may miss representation recoverable by deeper decoders; a heavier readout control is needed for the strong claim.
default_community_belief: A diffusion model that generates as well as before is assumed to represent as well as before.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may mostly modify cross-attention and normalization parameters, leaving spatial features and their segmentation utility intact.
fastest_falsification: Probe comparison between a base model and its public step-distilled variant, one day.

one_line: Diffusion-feature segmenters fail predictably in regions the generator cannot generate well: generability maps forecast failure geography before any labels exist.
problem: When diffusion features are used for segmentation, there is no account of where they should be weak; failure analysis is post hoc and label-dependent.
core_hypothesis: Feature quality is tied to generation competence: regions with high reconstruction error under the generator (poorly modeled content) yield degraded features, so an unsupervised generability map computed from reconstruction quality predicts downstream segmentation error without access to labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-region reconstruction error of the underlying generator will correlate significantly with segmentation error of feature-based readouts across datasets, and the correlation will be specific (weaker for segmenters built on non-generative backbones on the same images).
why_important: Label-free failure forecasting would enable targeted annotation and safe-deployment gating for feature-based pipelines, and it tests the foundational claim that generative competence and representational competence are coupled at region level.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: coupling of generation and representation is assumed globally; a region-level predictive validation with cross-backbone specificity controls appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute reconstruction-error maps and diffusion-feature segmentation errors on two datasets, measure region-level correlation, and run the non-generative-backbone specificity control.
main_risk: Both quantities correlate with generic image complexity; the specificity control and complexity covariates are essential to avoid rediscovering that hard regions are hard.
default_community_belief: Failure locations of learned segmenters are idiosyncratic and require labeled validation data to discover.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature readouts may be robust to moderate generative incompetence, breaking the coupling everywhere except extreme out-of-distribution content.
fastest_falsification: Region-level correlation analysis on cached predictions, hours after feature extraction.

one_line: Emergent correspondence in diffusion features is instance-blind: on scenes with repeated objects it matches category, not instance, corrupting correspondence-based segmentation propagation.
problem: Diffusion features exhibit emergent semantic correspondence used for label propagation and video segmentation, but evaluation sets rarely stress repeated identical objects where instance identity matters.
core_hypothesis: Generative pretraining rewards category-level appearance modeling with no pressure for instance discrimination, so correspondence fields on repeated-object scenes collapse across instances, and propagation-based segmentation using these features will merge or swap instances at rates far above appearance-based trackers.
falsifiable_prediction: On constructed repeated-object benchmarks, diffusion-feature correspondence will match to the wrong instance significantly more often than self-supervised tracking features at matched category accuracy, with error rate increasing with instance count and symmetry.
why_important: Correspondence propagation is a core building block for cheap video and interactive segmentation; instance blindness defines a hard applicability boundary that current benchmark averages conceal.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: emergent correspondence quality is documented on standard pairs; systematic repeated-object stress testing with instance-error decomposition appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a repeated-object correspondence set (arrays of identical items with ground-truth instance identity), evaluate diffusion versus tracking features, and decompose errors into category and instance components.
main_risk: Position encodings in extraction pipelines may partially rescue instance matching, so the effect size depends on implementation details that must be reported per pipeline.
default_community_belief: Emergent diffusion correspondence is treated as approaching general-purpose matching quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Local context differences around each instance may suffice for correct matching even without instance-aware features.
fastest_falsification: Small repeated-object benchmark from existing instance datasets, evaluation in one day.

one_line: Text conditioning is a hidden test-time variable in diffusion-feature segmentation: changing an ostensibly irrelevant prompt flips downstream mask decisions.
problem: Diffusion feature extraction pipelines condition on some prompt (empty, generic, or class-related), treated as an implementation detail rather than an input that changes the answer.
core_hypothesis: Conditioning shifts feature geometry globally, not just at prompt-relevant regions, so segmentation readouts built on these features change decisions on objects unrelated to the prompt, making reported results prompt-specific in unacknowledged ways.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a set of semantically unrelated prompts, per-pixel decision flip rates of a frozen feature-based segmenter will substantially exceed seed-level noise, including on objects never mentioned, and flip rate will correlate with prompt embedding distance.
why_important: If prompt choice functions as an invisible hyperparameter, cross-paper comparisons of diffusion-feature methods are confounded, and deployment behavior can change through prompt template edits that pass no code review as model changes.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: prompt sensitivity is studied for generation; its propagation through features into segmentation decisions on unrelated content appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix images and readout, sweep ten unrelated prompts, and quantify flip rates against multi-seed baselines on prompt-unrelated objects.
main_risk: Some pipelines use unconditional extraction where the effect is zero by construction; the scope must be mapped across popular implementations.
default_community_belief: The extraction prompt is a neutral implementation detail as long as it is held fixed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cross-attention contributions may be small enough at feature-extraction layers that flips stay within noise for realistic prompts.
fastest_falsification: Prompt-sweep flip-rate measurement on one pipeline, hours.

one_line: Generative priors impose a closed vocabulary through the back door: objects the generator cannot synthesize get feature-assimilated to their nearest generable category.
problem: Diffusion features are marketed as open-vocabulary-friendly, but the generator was trained on a finite concept distribution; how truly novel objects are represented is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: For objects outside the generator's synthesis competence, features are constructed by analogy to the nearest generable concepts, so novel-object features lie inside familiar-category regions of feature space, and segmentation readouts label novel objects as coherent wrong categories rather than as unknown or fragmented.
falsifiable_prediction: On genuinely novel object sets (new industrial parts, rare artifacts), diffusion-feature segmenters will produce confident single-category assimilation errors at higher rates than discriminative-feature counterparts, and assimilation targets will be predictable from generation-based nearest-concept queries.
why_important: Coherent confident mislabeling is more dangerous than fragmentation for open-world deployment, and the predictability of assimilation targets would give a concrete audit: query the generator to forecast how novel objects will be mislabeled.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: open-vocabulary limits are discussed for CLIP-like models; a generative-assimilation account with target-prediction validation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble novel-object images verified as poorly generable, compare error structure (assimilation versus fragmentation) across feature families, and test target predictability via generator-based retrieval.
main_risk: Verifying that objects are truly outside generative competence, rather than merely rare, requires careful generation-based screening.
default_community_belief: Rich generative pretraining yields features that represent arbitrary new objects compositionally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compositional generalization in large diffusion models may be strong enough that genuinely non-generable objects are vanishingly rare in practice.
fastest_falsification: Error-structure comparison on one novel-parts dataset, two days including screening.

one_line: Averaging diffusion features across timesteps helps segmentation because different timesteps segment different semantic granularities, not because averaging reduces noise.
problem: Multi-timestep feature fusion empirically outperforms single timesteps, and the gain is attributed vaguely to ensembling; the mechanism is untested.
core_hypothesis: Each timestep's features induce a partition at a characteristic granularity (parts at low noise, objects at mid, regions at high); fusion wins by covering the granularity hierarchy, so gains should be reproducible by explicit hierarchy-aware selection and should vanish when all timesteps are forced to one granularity.
falsifiable_prediction: Clustering features per timestep will yield partitions whose granularity (segment count, hierarchy consistency) shifts monotonically with noise level; a granularity-matched fusion ablation will retain most of the multi-timestep gain while a variance-reduction control (multi-seed same-timestep averaging) will retain little.
why_important: Mechanistic understanding turns an empirical trick into a design principle: readouts could select timesteps per query granularity, and the granularity hierarchy itself becomes an unsupervised scene-parsing signal.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: multi-timestep fusion is common practice; the granularity-decomposition explanation with matched controls appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Per-timestep unsupervised partitions on one dataset, granularity metrics versus noise level, then the two fusion ablations (granularity-matched versus multi-seed variance control).
main_risk: Granularity may vary more across layers than timesteps, requiring joint analysis to attribute the effect correctly.
default_community_belief: Multi-timestep fusion is a variance-reduction ensemble over noisy feature estimates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gains might come from a single best timestep per image (selection effect) rather than complementary granularities.
fastest_falsification: Multi-seed same-timestep control versus multi-timestep fusion, one day.

one_line: Latent-space autoencoders in latent diffusion impose a hard minimum resolvable structure size, creating a resolution floor no decoder fine-tuning can cross for segmentation through latents.
problem: Latent diffusion pipelines (features, restoration, mask generation) route everything through a spatially downsampled VAE; the community treats the autoencoder as visually lossless without characterizing its structural information loss.
core_hypothesis: Structures thinner than a threshold tied to the latent downsampling factor are represented only as texture statistics, not as localizable entities; their exact geometry is unrecoverable from latents, so any latent-space segmentation or restoration has a provable thin-structure floor, measurable as chance-level localization below the threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: Reconstruction and probing experiments will show localization accuracy for inserted thin structures collapsing to chance below a width threshold that scales with the latent factor (8x versus 4x autoencoders shifting the threshold proportionally), regardless of decoder fine-tuning effort.
why_important: A quantified floor tells the field which applications (vessels, wires, microscopy filaments) are structurally incompatible with latent-space pipelines, preventing wasted engineering and mis-trusted outputs.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: VAE reconstruction artifacts are known qualitatively; a scaling law for structural information loss versus latent factor, validated with probing rather than pixel metrics, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert calibrated thin structures, encode-decode with autoencoders of different latent factors, probe latents for structure position, and map the localization threshold as a function of factor.
main_risk: Some information may survive in high-frequency latent channels in ways probes miss; a decoder-retraining upper-bound control is needed to claim unrecoverability.
default_community_belief: Latent autoencoders are effectively lossless for downstream purposes because reconstructions look excellent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned decoders may exploit context to re-localize thin structures accurately, making the floor softer than the information argument suggests.
fastest_falsification: Thin-structure insertion and reconstruction localization test on public autoencoders, one day.

one_line: Diffusion segmentation models sample plausible masks, not posterior samples: their mask distribution is measurably under-dispersed relative to annotator distributions.
problem: Diffusion-based segmentation is promoted as sampling from the mask posterior given the image, but the claim is validated with diversity metrics that cannot distinguish posterior fidelity from stylized variability.
core_hypothesis: Training dynamics and guidance push mask diffusion toward high-density plausible modes, so the sampled distribution is systematically narrower than the true conditional (annotator) distribution, with rare-but-valid interpretations underrepresented by large factors.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-annotator datasets, coverage tests will show annotator masks falling outside the sampled distribution's support far more often than exchangeability predicts, with mode-level interpretations present in annotations but absent from hundreds of samples.
why_important: Downstream uses (risk estimates, treatment margins, active learning) consume these samples as posterior draws; under-dispersion silently converts calibrated-looking pipelines into overconfident ones at the distribution level, a different and worse defect than pointwise miscalibration.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: diversity of diffusion segmentation is reported via GED-style scores; formal coverage testing against annotator distributions with mode-level analysis appears rare, pending literature check.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample extensively from one published mask-diffusion model on a multi-annotator dataset and run rank-based coverage tests of annotator masks within sample populations.
main_risk: Few public datasets have enough annotators per image for well-powered coverage tests; pooling strategies must avoid conflating inter-image and intra-image variability.
default_community_belief: Multi-sample diffusion segmentation approximates the conditional distribution over valid masks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some models may actually be over-dispersed at boundaries, offsetting mode-level narrowness in aggregate tests unless components are separated.
fastest_falsification: Coverage test on one dataset-model pair with existing checkpoints, one day including sampling.

one_line: The celebrated diversity of diffusion segmentation is boundary jitter, not hypothesis-level diversity: samples rarely differ in topology or structure the way annotators do.
problem: Sample diversity is quantified by pixel-level distances that cannot distinguish jittered contours from genuinely different interpretations (include-or-exclude a structure, split-or-merge decisions).
core_hypothesis: Noise injection in mask diffusion perturbs contours locally, whereas annotator disagreement is dominated by discrete structural choices; decomposing sample variability into boundary-jitter and structural components will show models concentrated in jitter while annotators concentrate in structure.
falsifiable_prediction: Using a decomposition into topology-changing and boundary-displacement variation, the structural share of model-sample variance will be several times smaller than the structural share of annotator variance on the same images.
why_important: If model diversity is the wrong kind of diversity, applications that need interpretation alternatives (surgical planning, ambiguity flagging) receive cosmetic variation instead, and diversity metrics rewarding jitter have been optimizing the wrong target.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: a jitter-versus-structure decomposition of segmentation sample diversity, applied to both models and annotators, appears not to be standard methodology.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define the decomposition (connected-component and topology signature changes versus contour displacement), apply to samples and annotations on one multi-rater dataset, and compare shares.
main_risk: The decomposition boundary is definitional; results must be shown robust to reasonable choices of what counts as structural change.
default_community_belief: High inter-sample variability means the model captures annotation ambiguity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conditioning architectures with strong stochastic latents may genuinely produce structural alternatives on some datasets, making the deficit model-specific rather than paradigm-wide.
fastest_falsification: Topology-signature variance comparison on existing samples versus annotations, hours.

one_line: The argmax decoding step at the end of mask diffusion destroys the learned distribution, and decoding choice changes reported accuracy more than most architectural contributions.
problem: Continuous mask diffusion ends with an arbitrary discretization (threshold, argmax, majority vote over samples) that is barely reported, though it maps a distribution to a point estimate.
core_hypothesis: Different decoding rules (single-sample argmax, mean-then-threshold, per-pixel majority, loss-aware Bayes decoding) select different points of the learned distribution with systematically different error profiles, and the induced metric differences exceed typical published architecture deltas.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-decoding the same trained model's samples under four rules will produce mIoU and boundary-F spreads larger than the median improvement claimed by recent mask-diffusion papers over their baselines, with rule rankings flipping between region and boundary metrics.
why_important: If decoding dominates architecture, part of the literature's progress signal is decoding-rule noise, and fair comparison requires standardized, loss-matched decoding, analogous to decoding standardization in machine translation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: Bayes-optimal decoding under task losses is classical theory; its empirical impact accounting for mask-diffusion literature comparisons appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take two public mask-diffusion checkpoints, fix samples, sweep decoding rules, and compare the induced metric spread with published improvement margins.
main_risk: Public checkpoints for this family are scarcer than papers; partial reproduction may be needed, adding training variance to the comparison.
default_community_belief: Final mask extraction is a detail; reported gains reflect modeling improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On easy benchmarks the distribution may be concentrated enough that all reasonable decodings agree, confining the effect to ambiguous data.
fastest_falsification: Decoding-rule sweep over cached samples, hours.

one_line: The denoising trajectory of mask diffusion reveals a consistent coarse-to-fine part hierarchy, providing an unsupervised scene-parsing signal in the order structures emerge.
problem: Only the endpoint of mask-diffusion trajectories is used; whether the emergence order of structures along the trajectory is stable and meaningful is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Global object layout stabilizes early in denoising and finer parts crystallize progressively, and this ordering is consistent across seeds and images within a category, so emergence time functions as an unsupervised hierarchy index over segments.
falsifiable_prediction: Emergence-time orderings of segments will be strongly rank-correlated across seeds for the same image, and hierarchy trees derived from emergence times will agree with human part-whole annotations substantially above chance on part-annotated datasets.
why_important: It would extract structured scene grammar from a model trained only on flat masks, suggesting diffusion training discovers compositional structure as an inductive consequence of multi-scale denoising, a scientifically interesting emergence claim.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: trajectory analysis exists for image generation; using mask-diffusion emergence order as a part-hierarchy extractor appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument trajectories of a trained mask-diffusion model, compute per-segment emergence times over seeds, and evaluate derived hierarchies against part annotations.
main_risk: Emergence order may reflect segment size alone; size-controlled analysis is needed to show the hierarchy is more than a scale artifact.
default_community_belief: Intermediate diffusion states are noisy transients without independent semantic content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Trajectories may be chaotic at segment level even when endpoints agree, destroying cross-seed ordering consistency.
fastest_falsification: Cross-seed emergence-order correlation on one model and dataset, one day.

one_line: Most trained mask-diffusion models are secretly deterministic: their output barely depends on the noise input, making the diffusion machinery dead weight at inference.
problem: Mask diffusion carries multi-step stochastic machinery whose contribution is assumed; effective stochasticity after training on strongly conditioned tasks is not measured.
core_hypothesis: With strong image conditioning and mask targets that are nearly deterministic given the image, training collapses the model onto a conditional mean function; inter-seed output variance shrinks toward numerical noise, and a distilled one-step deterministic student matches the full sampler.
falsifiable_prediction: For published mask-diffusion models on standard (single-annotator) benchmarks, inter-seed mask variance will be an order of magnitude below inter-image variance, and single-step distillation will match multi-step sampling within seed-level noise on all metrics.
why_important: If the stochastic process contributes nothing, the field is paying large inference costs and claiming distributional semantics for what is functionally a deterministic segmenter, and the honest comparison baseline should be deterministic architectures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: stochasticity collapse is suspected informally; a systematic effective-stochasticity audit across published mask-diffusion models appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure inter-seed variance for two or three public checkpoints on their benchmarks and attempt one-step distillation, comparing metric parity.
main_risk: Conclusions will vary with dataset ambiguity; the claim must be scoped to single-annotator benchmarks where it is most damning.
default_community_belief: The iterative stochastic process is integral to mask-diffusion performance and semantics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some checkpoints may retain genuine multimodality at object-presence level that seed-variance summaries underweight.
fastest_falsification: Inter-seed variance audit on one public checkpoint, hours.

one_line: More denoising steps can make segmentation masks worse: mask quality is non-monotonic in sampling steps because later steps impose the mask prior over image evidence.
problem: Sampling-step count is tuned for image generation where more steps help fidelity; mask diffusion inherits the more-steps-is-better assumption without task-specific analysis.
core_hypothesis: Early steps incorporate image evidence while later steps refine toward the learned mask distribution (smoothness, shape regularity); past an optimum, refinement overwrites evidence-driven irregular details, so boundary accuracy peaks at moderate step counts and declines with further steps, especially for irregular objects.
falsifiable_prediction: Step-count sweeps will show boundary F-score peaking at intermediate steps and declining thereafter, with the decline concentrated on objects whose true shapes are irregular relative to the dataset's shape statistics.
why_important: It exposes a prior-versus-evidence imbalance in the sampling procedure itself, implying compute reductions with accuracy gains, and predicts which content is harmed by the standard many-step recipes.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: step-quality curves exist for generation; a shape-regularity-conditioned non-monotonicity analysis for segmentation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep step counts on one trained model, stratify boundary metrics by object shape irregularity, and test for the predicted interaction.
main_risk: Schedulers confound step count with noise-level placement; multiple scheduler families must be tested to isolate the effect.
default_community_belief: More sampling steps give equal or better masks, with compute as the only cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong conditioning throughout the trajectory may keep evidence dominant at every step, making quality flat rather than peaked.
fastest_falsification: Step-sweep with shape stratification on an existing model, hours.

one_line: The standard denoising objective mis-weights segmentation errors by object area, predictably sacrificing small objects relative to discriminative training at matched capacity.
problem: Mask diffusion trains with pixelwise reconstruction of noised masks, whereas segmentation quality is measured by overlap metrics that weight small objects heavily; the loss-metric geometry mismatch is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Under pixel-summed denoising loss, a small object's total gradient contribution scales with its area, so optimization tolerates whole-small-object failures at costs that overlap metrics punish severely; mask diffusion therefore shows a characteristic small-object recall deficit versus discriminative models trained with frequency-balanced losses.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched backbone and data, per-size-bin comparison will show mask diffusion trailing discriminative baselines specifically in the smallest bins, and reweighting the denoising loss by instance area will close most of that specific gap without helping large objects.
why_important: It identifies a structural, fixable cause for a performance pattern likely to be misattributed to the generative paradigm itself, informing whether the paradigm or its default loss is deficient.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: loss imbalance is well studied for discriminative segmentation; its manifestation and correction inside diffusion objectives appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small matched models (diffusion versus discriminative) on one dataset, compare size-binned recall, then retrain diffusion with area-reweighted loss and verify selective improvement.
main_risk: Full-scale training is expensive; small-model conclusions may not transfer to large regimes, requiring at least one scale-check run.
default_community_belief: Mask diffusion under-performance where observed reflects immaturity of the paradigm rather than an analyzable loss-geometry artifact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multi-scale U-Net inductive biases might compensate for the loss weighting, leaving no size-specific gap to explain.
fastest_falsification: Size-binned evaluation of existing published models against discriminative baselines on shared benchmarks, hours if predictions are released.

one_line: Image-conditioned mask diffusion decides mask layout from the dataset prior early in the trajectory, consulting the image mainly for late refinement: conditioning arrives too late.
problem: It is assumed the conditioning image guides the entire denoising trajectory; when conditioning information actually enters the developing mask is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: At high noise, mask hypotheses are shaped predominantly by the learned unconditional mask distribution (typical layouts, sizes, positions); image evidence dominates only at low noise, so early-trajectory errors reflecting dataset layout priors persist to the final mask when late refinement cannot undo global commitments.
falsifiable_prediction: Swapping the conditioning image mid-trajectory will show a sharp transition timestep after which the final mask follows the new image locally but retains the first image's global layout, and final-error locations will be predicted by divergence between the test layout and dataset layout statistics.
why_important: A late-arriving conditioning pathology would explain systematic failures on atypical layouts (off-center objects, unusual scales) and motivate noise-dependent conditioning strength as a principled fix, rather than more capacity.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: mid-trajectory swap experiments exist for text-to-image analysis; applying them to quantify conditioning latency in segmentation diffusion appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run conditioning-swap experiments across timesteps on one trained model and measure layout inheritance versus local content adoption in final masks.
main_risk: Swap experiments perturb the trajectory off-distribution; results need corroboration by attention-flow or gradient attribution along unperturbed trajectories.
default_community_belief: Conditioning guides denoising uniformly from the first step onward.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong cross-attention at all noise levels may make layout image-driven from the start, with atypical-layout failures explained by data scarcity instead.
fastest_falsification: Layout-atypicality versus error correlation on existing predictions, hours; swap experiment, one day.

one_line: Inpainting-style local mask editing with diffusion models is nonlocal: correcting one region measurably changes distant, untouched regions of the mask.
problem: Interactive correction with mask diffusion resamples a region conditioned on the rest, assuming edits stay local; the model's global shape prior may not respect the edit boundary.
core_hypothesis: Because the learned mask prior couples distant structure (symmetry, object counts, closure), region-resampling propagates changes beyond the edit mask, so repeated local corrections perturb previously approved regions, undermining the audit logic of human-in-the-loop workflows.
falsifiable_prediction: Edit-locality measurements will show statistically significant changes outside edit regions exceeding re-sampling noise baselines, growing with the prior-coupling strength of the content (symmetric and repeated structures worst), and accumulating over sequential edit rounds.
why_important: Interactive medical and mapping workflows certify masks region by region; nonlocal edit propagation silently invalidates prior certifications, a workflow-safety issue no aggregate accuracy metric detects.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: nonlocal effects of diffusion inpainting are known anecdotally for images; quantified edit-locality analysis for segmentation correction workflows appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Perform scripted local edits on one interactive mask-diffusion system, measure out-of-region change against multi-seed baselines, and track accumulation over edit sequences.
main_risk: Distinguishing prior-coupling propagation from mere sampling variance requires careful matched-seed protocols.
default_community_belief: Conditioned resampling of a region leaves the complement unchanged by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Implementations that hard-freeze the complement in every step may keep changes strictly local, confining the effect to soft-conditioning variants.
fastest_falsification: Out-of-region change measurement on one implementation, hours.

one_line: Continuous relaxation of categorical masks in diffusion biases boundary placement systematically compared to discrete diffusion, an unexamined determinant of boundary metrics.
problem: Mask diffusion mostly embeds discrete labels into continuous space for Gaussian noising, assuming the relaxation is semantically neutral; discrete (categorical) diffusion formulations exist but boundary-level behavioral comparisons are absent.
core_hypothesis: Gaussian noising of label embeddings creates intermediate values that decode asymmetrically near class boundaries (favoring classes whose embeddings dominate mixture midpoints), so continuous-relaxation models place boundaries with a class-pair-specific bias that discrete diffusion does not share.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched training, signed boundary displacement per class pair will differ systematically between continuous and discrete mask diffusion, with the continuous bias predictable from embedding geometry (midpoint decoding analysis), and per-pair biases will flip when embedding assignments are permuted.
why_important: If representation choice injects class-pair boundary bias, reported boundary improvements across papers partly reflect embedding choices, and safety-relevant boundary decisions inherit an arbitrary artifact controllable at design time.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: discrete-versus-continuous diffusion is compared on likelihoods and sample quality; a boundary-placement bias analysis tied to embedding geometry appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small continuous and discrete mask-diffusion models on one dataset, measure signed per-class-pair boundary displacement, and run the embedding-permutation control.
main_risk: Small-model training noise may swamp per-pair signals; multiple seeds and paired statistics are required.
default_community_belief: How masks are embedded for diffusion is an implementation detail without semantic consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoders may learn to compensate for embedding asymmetries, leaving no net bias at convergence.
fastest_falsification: Midpoint-decoding analysis of a trained continuous model (no retraining), one day.

one_line: Sample-variance maps from diffusion segmentation at practical sample counts measure sampler noise, not ambiguity: the variance map barely changes when ambiguity does.
problem: Per-pixel variance over a handful of diffusion samples is presented as an ambiguity or uncertainty map, without validating its sensitivity to actual ambiguity manipulations at deployment-realistic sample counts.
core_hypothesis: At the 4-10 samples used in practice, variance estimates are dominated by sampler stochasticity and discretization noise; the maps will be nearly invariant when image ambiguity is experimentally increased or decreased, revealing them as sampler diagnostics rather than ambiguity measurements.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled ambiguity manipulations (progressive occlusion, contrast reduction at specific boundaries) will change annotator disagreement strongly but leave small-sample variance maps statistically unchanged outside trivial boundary widening, while 100+ samples are needed before the maps track the manipulation.
why_important: This targets the methodology of a growing literature: if practical-variance maps are insensitive to the quantity they claim to measure, papers validating them by visual plausibility are systematically misled, independent of any calibration question.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: sample-size effects on variance estimates are elementary statistics, but an ambiguity-manipulation sensitivity audit of diffusion segmentation variance maps appears undone; framed here as diffusion-methodology science, not calibration research.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design graded ambiguity manipulations on real images, collect small-N and large-N sample variance maps from one model, and test sensitivity of each against the manipulation strength.
main_risk: Ambiguity manipulations must not trivially change image difficulty overall; localized manipulations with matched global statistics are needed.
default_community_belief: Inter-sample variance of diffusion segmentation is a usable ambiguity map at the sample counts papers actually use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For some models sampler noise may itself concentrate at ambiguous pixels, accidentally making small-N maps informative.
fastest_falsification: Small-N versus large-N map stability analysis on one model, hours.

one_line: Classifier-free guidance strength in conditional mask diffusion is an undisclosed precision-recall knob, making cross-paper comparisons at unspecified guidance meaningless.
problem: Guidance scale is tuned per paper and rarely analyzed; its systematic effect on segmentation error structure is unknown, unlike its well-studied fidelity-diversity effect in generation.
core_hypothesis: Increasing guidance sharpens commitment to high-conditional-density masks, monotonically trading recall of uncertain structures for precision on confident ones; each guidance value is thus a different operating point on a precision-recall curve, and papers comparing at different scales compare operating points, not models.
falsifiable_prediction: Guidance sweeps will trace smooth monotonic precision-recall curves for multiple models and datasets, with published per-paper settings scattering across the curve such that observed cross-paper metric differences can be substantially reproduced by guidance adjustment alone.
why_important: An unreported operating-point parameter that moves headline metrics corrupts the literature's comparative signal, and once characterized, guidance becomes a free deployment knob for matching clinical or industrial precision-recall requirements without retraining.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: guidance effects are characterized for generation quality; a precision-recall operating-point account for segmentation with cross-paper reanalysis appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep guidance on two conditional mask-diffusion models across two datasets, plot precision-recall trajectories, and reanalyze published comparisons where checkpoints exist.
main_risk: Some formulations bake conditioning without CFG; the scope covers only guidance-based variants and must say so explicitly.
default_community_belief: Guidance scale is a stability hyperparameter whose exact value is a minor reproducibility detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For strongly image-conditioned tasks, guidance may saturate quickly, compressing the operating range into insignificance.
fastest_falsification: Guidance sweep on one public model, hours.

one_line: Self-conditioning in mask diffusion causes error lock-in: mistakes made early in the trajectory persist to the final mask instead of being iteratively refined away.
problem: Self-conditioning (feeding the current mask estimate into subsequent steps) is credited for quality gains under an iterative-refinement narrative; whether it also entrenches early errors is untested.
core_hypothesis: Self-conditioning creates a positive feedback loop in which early erroneous commitments are treated as evidence by later steps; the probability that an error present at the trajectory's first quarter survives to the final mask is far higher with self-conditioning than without, especially for object-presence errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-persistence tracking will show survival rates of early errors significantly higher in self-conditioned models than in matched non-self-conditioned models, and injecting controlled early errors into the self-conditioning channel will reproduce them in final masks at high rates.
why_important: It replaces the refinement narrative with a commit-and-defend account for a widely adopted mechanism, explaining stubborn hallucinated or missing objects and motivating scheduled self-conditioning dropout as a principled remedy.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: self-conditioning is evaluated by endpoint metrics only; trajectory-level error-persistence analysis with causal injection appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without self-conditioning on one dataset, instrument trajectories, measure early-error survival, and run the error-injection intervention.
main_risk: Matched training is required because self-conditioning changes convergence; compute cost is moderate but non-trivial.
default_community_belief: Iterative denoising with self-conditioning progressively corrects errors, which is why it improves benchmarks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmark gains may come precisely from persistence of good early decisions, with error lock-in rare enough to be a net win regardless.
fastest_falsification: Error-injection experiment on an existing self-conditioned checkpoint, one day.

one_line: Denoising-pretrained and inpainting-pretrained models transfer to segmentation with dissociable failure modes: boundary-sharpening false positives versus region-completion false negatives.
problem: Generative pretraining objectives are compared by downstream accuracy scalars, obscuring whether different objectives install different error structures in the fine-tuned segmenter.
core_hypothesis: Denoising pretraining rewards recovering sharp local statistics, biasing transferred models toward over-detection of boundary-like structure; masked inpainting rewards plausible region filling, biasing them toward completing regions over evidence and missing internal discontinuities; the two produce mirror-image error profiles at matched aggregate accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched mIoU after identical fine-tuning, denoising-pretrained models will show significantly higher boundary false-positive rates and inpainting-pretrained models higher internal-discontinuity miss rates, consistent across two datasets and two backbone sizes.
why_important: If pretraining objective selects the failure mode, practitioners can choose backbones by which errors their application tolerates, and objective mixtures become a targeted design tool rather than an ablation curiosity.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: objective comparisons report scalar transfer quality; a failure-mode dissociation account with mirror-error predictions appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune matched denoising- and inpainting-pretrained backbones on one dataset and compare structured error profiles (boundary FP, discontinuity FN) at matched aggregate accuracy.
main_risk: Publicly available pretrained pairs differ in data and scale; controlled same-data pretraining at small scale may be needed for a clean claim.
default_community_belief: Better generative pretraining yields uniformly better transfer; objectives differ in strength, not in error character.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may wash out objective-specific biases entirely given enough labeled data, leaving dissociation visible only in few-shot regimes.
fastest_falsification: Structured-error comparison of existing public checkpoints fine-tuned identically, two days.

one_line: Task utility is a third axis of the perception-distortion tradeoff that is non-monotonic in both: segmentation utility peaks at interior points no image metric identifies.
problem: Restoration methods are placed on a perception-distortion plane, and downstream users pick models assuming utility improves along one of the two axes.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation utility is maximized at intermediate perception-distortion combinations (some distortion tolerated for evidence faithfulness, some perceptual quality needed for feature compatibility), so the utility-optimal operating point lies strictly inside the perception-distortion frontier region and cannot be found by optimizing either image metric.
falsifiable_prediction: Mapping utility over a grid of restoration operating points (varying perceptual-loss weight) will show an interior maximum, with utility at both frontier extremes (pure distortion-optimal and pure perception-optimal) measurably below the interior peak on at least two datasets.
why_important: The perception-distortion framework guides restoration research; establishing a non-monotonic utility axis redefines what restoration should optimize for machine consumption and explains contradictory reports about whether restoration helps downstream tasks.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the perception-distortion tradeoff is established theory and task effects are studied piecemeal; a mapped utility surface with interior-maximum demonstration appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or collect restorers spanning the perceptual-weight axis, evaluate one frozen segmenter across the grid at fixed degradation, and locate the utility maximum relative to the frontier extremes.
main_risk: The interior peak may be shallow relative to evaluation noise, requiring many seeds for a decisive answer.
default_community_belief: Downstream utility improves monotonically with either lower distortion or better perceptual quality, depending on the task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For robust modern segmenters, utility may be flat across the entire frontier, making the choice irrelevant rather than non-monotonic.
fastest_falsification: Utility evaluation across existing checkpoints spanning the perceptual-weight axis (distortion-oriented and GAN-oriented variants of one SR family), one day.

one_line: Restorations matched on FID differ widely in downstream segmentation accuracy: distribution-level metrics are blind to the task-relevant differences between restorers.
problem: Distribution metrics like FID are used to rank generative restorers under the assumption that distributional realism proxies usefulness.
core_hypothesis: FID measures aggregate feature-distribution alignment while segmentation depends on per-image evidence fidelity at boundaries and small structures; two restorers can be FID-equivalent while differing by large margins in utility, so FID rank and utility rank will decorrelate across restorer families.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of restorers spanning architectures, correlation between FID and downstream mIoU will be weak and family-dependent, and pairs of models matched on FID within noise will show utility gaps larger than typical published method deltas.
why_important: Restoration model selection for pipelines is often FID-driven; demonstrating decorrelation forces utility-based selection protocols and undermines FID-based claims of downstream readiness.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: FID criticisms exist for generation; a systematic FID-versus-segmentation-utility decorrelation study across restorer families appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate ten restorers on one degraded benchmark for both FID and frozen-segmenter utility, compute rank correlation, and identify FID-matched utility-discordant pairs.
main_risk: Restorer pools may confound architecture with training data; conclusions should be conditioned on documented training setups.
default_community_belief: Lower FID indicates a better restorer for downstream applications, not just for human viewing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Within a single restorer family at fixed data, FID and utility may correlate well, making the decorrelation a cross-family artifact of limited practical relevance.
fastest_falsification: FID-versus-utility scatter over public checkpoints, one day.

one_line: Human preference between restorations anti-predicts machine utility in identifiable regimes: raters prefer smooth denoised outputs that segmenters do worse on.
problem: Human studies are the gold standard for restoration quality, and pipelines assume the human-preferred output is also the better machine input.
core_hypothesis: Human preference penalizes residual noise strongly and hallucinated smoothness weakly, while segmentation accuracy shows the opposite sensitivities; in the noise-versus-smoothness regime, preference and utility will be negatively correlated, not merely uncorrelated.
falsifiable_prediction: Two-alternative human choices between noisy-sharp and smooth-denoised restorations of the same inputs will favor smooth outputs, while a frozen segmenter scores higher on the noisy-sharp alternatives, yielding a significant negative preference-utility association within this regime.
why_important: Anti-correlation (not just decorrelation) means human-in-the-loop quality control actively selects worse pipeline configurations for machine consumption, a concrete operational hazard for hybrid workflows.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: human-machine metric divergence is discussed broadly; a regime-scoped demonstration of sign-reversed association for segmentation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct matched restoration pairs along the noise-smoothness axis, run a small preference study, evaluate utility with a frozen segmenter, and test the association's sign within regime.
main_risk: Preference depends on viewing conditions and instructions; the study must standardize zoom and task framing to be reproducible.
default_community_belief: Human preference is a safe proxy for downstream machine utility of restored images.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Preference instructions emphasizing detail preservation may realign raters with machine utility, showing the divergence is protocol-dependent rather than fundamental.
fastest_falsification: Reuse any published preference dataset with references, evaluate utility on the same pairs, compute association, hours to days.

one_line: The utility-optimal restoration depends on which segmentation metric will be used: boundary-metric consumers need different restorations than region-metric consumers.
problem: Restoration is tuned once and assumed good for the downstream task, but the downstream task's own evaluation metric (region overlap versus boundary quality) values different image properties.
core_hypothesis: Restoration operating points that maximize mIoU differ systematically from those maximizing boundary F-score: region metrics tolerate smoothing that boundary metrics punish, so the utility ranking of restorers reverses when the downstream metric changes, making metric-unaware restoration tuning ill-posed.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a restoration operating-point sweep, the argmax operating points for mIoU and for boundary F-score will differ consistently (boundary metrics preferring higher-frequency preservation), with rank reversals among restorers between the two metrics on multiple datasets.
why_important: It shows restoration-for-vision cannot be a single product: pipeline builders must declare the downstream metric before choosing preprocessing, and papers claiming task-agnostic restoration benefits are implicitly metric-specific.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: metric sensitivity to smoothing is known qualitatively; a demonstrated restorer-ranking reversal between region and boundary metrics appears undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep restoration strength and style on one degraded dataset, evaluate a frozen segmenter under both metric families, and test for argmax divergence and rank reversals.
main_risk: If boundary and region optima coincide on most content, the effect may be limited to boundary-dense imagery, narrowing but not nullifying the claim.
default_community_belief: A well-restored image is well-restored for the task, regardless of how the task is scored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen segmenters may bottleneck both metrics identically, hiding any restoration-metric interaction that would appear with retrained heads.
fastest_falsification: Two-metric evaluation over an existing restoration sweep, hours.

one_line: Average distortion metrics hide class-conditional utility loss: restoration that improves overall image quality degrades minority-class segmentation, and the curves cross.
problem: Restoration quality is validated with pixel-averaged metrics dominated by majority content; whether all classes benefit equally is not asked.
core_hypothesis: Restoration priors are calibrated to frequent content, so quality gains concentrate on majority classes while rare-class evidence is regularized away; per-class utility-versus-restoration-strength curves therefore cross, with minority classes peaking at weaker restoration than majority classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class segmentation accuracy as a function of restoration strength will show significantly different peak locations by class frequency, with at least some minority classes strictly harmed at the strength that maximizes average utility.
why_important: Choosing restoration strength by average metrics then systematically sacrifices rare classes, which in medical, industrial, and ecological applications are the classes that matter; per-class restoration auditing becomes a deployment requirement.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: class imbalance is studied in training; its interaction with preprocessing strength as crossing utility curves appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep restoration strength on one imbalanced benchmark, plot per-class utility curves, and test peak-location dependence on class frequency.
main_risk: Per-class curves are noisier for rare classes by definition; adequate test-set sizes or aggregation across rare classes is needed.
default_community_belief: Preprocessing that raises average image quality raises, or at worst preserves, accuracy for every class.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rare-class evidence may be spatially co-located with majority-class evidence such that restoration treats them identically, keeping curves aligned.
fastest_falsification: Per-class utility evaluation across three restoration strengths on one dataset, hours.

one_line: Restoration helps segmentation only below an input-quality threshold and strictly hurts above it, and the community averages across regimes into a meaningless net effect.
problem: Contradictory findings on whether restoration preprocessing helps downstream tasks persist because studies aggregate over heterogeneous input-quality distributions.
core_hypothesis: The restoration effect on utility is piecewise: below a quality threshold, evidence recovery dominates and restoration helps; above it, prior imposition dominates and restoration hurts; the threshold is estimable per restorer-segmenter pair, and cross-study disagreement is explained by where each dataset sits relative to threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying any degraded dataset by estimated input quality will reveal a crossing point where the restoration effect changes sign, with the crossing reproducible across datasets for a fixed restorer-segmenter pair and shifted predictably when either component is swapped.
why_important: A quality-gated deployment rule (restore only below threshold) would replace blanket preprocessing policies, and the regime account resolves an apparent literature contradiction without accusing any study of error.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: conditional restoration policies exist in engineering; establishing and validating a sign-crossing threshold law as the explanation for contradictory published effects appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quality-stratified utility analysis on two degraded benchmarks with one restorer-segmenter pair, locating the sign crossing and testing cross-dataset consistency.
main_risk: No-reference quality estimation error blurs the threshold; using known synthetic severity as the quality axis first gives a clean version of the test.
default_community_belief: Restoration preprocessing has a characteristic net effect (helpful or harmful) that studies attempt to measure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The effect may vary continuously and weakly rather than crossing sign at a usable threshold, making the gating rule impractical.
fastest_falsification: Severity-stratified re-analysis of any existing restoration-utility experiment, hours if predictions are archived.

one_line: Task-aware restoration trained with segmentation losses learns to paint faint class-boundary contours into images rather than restoring them, so gains do not transfer to other segmenters.
problem: Task-driven restoration reports downstream gains without testing whether the front-end genuinely improves evidence or encodes decision hints readable only by its training-time partner.
core_hypothesis: Under joint or task-loss training, the cheapest optimization path is embedding low-amplitude contour cues at predicted class boundaries; such cue-painting yields large paired gains, weak transfer to independent segmenters, and detectable boundary-aligned structure in the restoration residual.
falsifiable_prediction: Residual analysis (restored minus distortion-only baseline) will show statistically significant energy aligned with predicted class boundaries; masking that residual component will collapse paired gains while barely affecting image quality metrics, and transfer gains to two unseen segmenters will be a small fraction of paired gains.
why_important: It distinguishes evidence restoration from covert task signaling, which determines whether task-aware restoration is a robust pipeline component or a brittle two-model entanglement that breaks on any downstream update.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: related collusion effects are reported in translation settings; residual-decomposition evidence for boundary painting in task-aware restoration appears missing.
