minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one task-aware restorer, decompose residuals against a distortion-matched control, mask boundary-aligned components, and measure paired versus transfer gains.
main_risk: Boundary-aligned residual energy can also arise from genuine edge restoration; the masking intervention and transfer tests are the discriminating evidence.
default_community_belief: Task-aware restoration improves the image in a task-relevant but model-agnostic way.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With strong image-quality regularization, cue-painting may be suppressed, making genuine enhancement the dominant mechanism after all.
fastest_falsification: Transfer-gap measurement for any published task-aware restorer against two independent segmenters, one day.

one_line: LPIPS-optimized restoration preferentially preserves classification-relevant information because LPIPS is built on classification features, measurably sacrificing the spatial precision dense tasks need.
problem: LPIPS is the default perceptual loss and metric for restoration, but its backbone was trained for classification, embedding a task bias into what counts as perceptually preserved.
core_hypothesis: Optimizing restoration toward LPIPS preserves texture and category-evidence statistics while tolerating spatial displacement of boundaries that classification features are invariant to; LPIPS-tuned restorers will therefore score high on classification-based probes but show boundary displacement measurably worse than distortion-tuned counterparts at matched LPIPS.
falsifiable_prediction: Across restorers, LPIPS will correlate with downstream classification accuracy but significantly less with boundary F-score; and boundary displacement of LPIPS-optimized restorations will exceed that of L1-optimized ones even when human raters judge them equal.
why_important: If the field's perceptual yardstick embeds classification invariances, restoration progress is being steered away from dense-prediction needs, explaining why perceptually impressive restorers disappoint in segmentation pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: LPIPS limitations are discussed; a task-bias account with boundary-displacement evidence and matched-LPIPS controls appears specific and untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare boundary displacement and dense-task utility of LPIPS-tuned versus L1-tuned restorations at matched LPIPS and matched human preference on one benchmark.
main_risk: Disentangling loss effects from architecture effects requires training pairs differing only in loss, a modest but real compute cost.
default_community_belief: LPIPS measures generic perceptual fidelity applicable to any downstream consumer of the image.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Classification backbones retain more spatial sensitivity than assumed, so LPIPS may penalize boundary displacement adequately in practice.
fastest_falsification: Boundary-displacement comparison on existing checkpoints trained with different losses, hours.

one_line: Human-optimized codecs misallocate bits against segmentation needs in a measurable, spatially structured way: utility-per-bit concentrates at boundaries that codecs deprioritize.
problem: Machine vision increasingly consumes images and video compressed for human viewing, but where task-relevant information sits relative to codec bit allocation has not been mapped.
core_hypothesis: Codecs spend bits on perceptually salient texture and luma structure while segmentation utility depends on precise boundary geometry and low-contrast region distinctions; the spatial correlation between codec bit allocation and marginal task utility is low or negative, implying large utility gains at equal bitrate from task-aware allocation.
falsifiable_prediction: Utility-per-bit maps (segmentation accuracy sensitivity to local quality, estimated by local quality perturbation) will correlate weakly or negatively with actual codec bit-density maps, and a re-allocation oracle at matched bitrate will recover a large fraction of degradation-induced accuracy loss.
why_important: It quantifies the cost of human-centric compression for machine pipelines and grounds machine-oriented coding standards in measured utility geography rather than intuition.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: video-coding-for-machines is an active standardization area; a spatial utility-per-bit versus bit-allocation correlation analysis for segmentation appears rare in the open literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute bit-density maps from codec internals for one benchmark, estimate utility sensitivity maps via local quality perturbation, correlate, and simulate oracle re-allocation.
main_risk: Utility sensitivity estimation via perturbation is approximate; two independent estimation methods should agree before conclusions are drawn.
default_community_belief: Perceptual bit allocation is close enough to task-optimal that machine consumers need only higher bitrates, not different allocation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary regions are often also perceptually salient, so allocation overlap may be higher than the hypothesis assumes.
fastest_falsification: Correlation of codec quantization maps with segmentation error maps on one compressed benchmark, one day.

one_line: No-reference IQA models have a structural blind spot for generative-restoration artifacts because they were trained on degradation artifacts, making them least reliable exactly where restoration pipelines need them.
problem: NR-IQA models are trained on databases of classical degradations (blur, noise, compression); generative restorers produce a different artifact family (semantic substitution, texture invention) that these models never saw.
core_hypothesis: NR-IQA models score generative-restoration outputs by their surface statistics, which are excellent by construction, so quality prediction error is systematically larger and biased upward on generatively restored images compared to classically degraded ones at matched true fidelity.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired data, the gap between NR-IQA predictions and reference-based fidelity will be significantly larger and positively biased for diffusion-restored images than for degraded or classically restored images, and fine-tuning NR-IQA on generative artifacts will remove most of the bias.
why_important: Pipelines use NR-IQA to gate restoration outputs into downstream analysis; an upward bias on generative outputs means exactly the riskiest images pass quality control, a structural monitoring hole in deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: NR-IQA domain gaps are known in principle; a quantified generative-artifact blind-spot analysis tied to pipeline gating risk appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched-fidelity sets of degraded, classically restored, and generatively restored images with references, and compare NR-IQA error distributions across the three families.
main_risk: Matching true fidelity across artifact families is nontrivial; reference-based fidelity must be multi-metric to avoid baking one definition into the conclusion.
default_community_belief: NR-IQA quality scores are artifact-family-agnostic measurements of image quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recent NR-IQA models trained with generative outputs in their corpora may already cover the artifact family, dating the blind spot.
fastest_falsification: NR-IQA error comparison across artifact families on one paired benchmark, hours.

one_line: Web-scraped segmentation datasets assembled after 2022 already contain diffusion-generated images, and this contamination measurably distorts benchmark conclusions.
problem: Dataset builders scrape the post-generative-AI web without screening for synthetic content, so modern benchmarks may silently mix real and generated imagery with unknown consequences for evaluation.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of recent scraped images are generator outputs; because generated images have simplified degradation statistics and prior-conformant structure, models score higher on the contaminated subset, inflating apparent progress and biasing cross-dataset conclusions toward generator-like imagery.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying synthetic-image detectors to recent scraped segmentation datasets will find a nonzero, dataset-dependent contamination rate; per-image accuracy will be significantly higher on detector-flagged images after controlling for content category, and removing them will shift reported model rankings on at least one benchmark.
why_important: Benchmarks are the field's measurement instrument; undetected synthetic admixture changes what is being measured, and the effect will grow every year, so the field needs contamination accounting now, before longitudinal comparisons become uninterpretable.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: contamination of language corpora is documented; a quantified audit for segmentation benchmarks with accuracy-impact analysis appears not yet published, pending literature search.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two independent synthetic-image detectors over one recent scraped benchmark, estimate contamination with false-positive calibration, and compare model accuracy on flagged versus unflagged subsets with content controls.
main_risk: Synthetic-image detectors have their own biases (style-correlated false positives); using multiple detectors and manual verification of samples is essential for a credible rate estimate.
default_community_belief: Benchmark images are real photographs; synthetic contamination is a hypothetical future problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Curation steps (source whitelists, date filters) in specific benchmarks may have excluded most synthetic content, making rates negligible for now.
fastest_falsification: Detector sweep over one dataset with manual spot-checks, two days.

one_line: Gains from diffusion-generated training data are partly artifact shortcuts: models key on generator fingerprints co-occurring with clean synthetic labels, and gains shrink when fingerprints are removed.
problem: Synthetic augmentation studies report accuracy gains without testing whether models exploit generator-specific artifacts as shortcut features tied to the perfectly consistent synthetic labels.
core_hypothesis: Generator outputs carry stable frequency-domain fingerprints; models learn joint features of fingerprint-plus-label regularities, so part of the measured synthetic-data gain reflects fingerprint-conditional processing rather than content learning, and will vanish under fingerprint-removal interventions.
falsifiable_prediction: Retraining with fingerprint-suppressed synthetic images (adversarial filtering or spectral normalization validated by detector failure) will reduce the synthetic-data gain by a significant fraction while leaving image content visually unchanged, and models trained on unfiltered data will show measurable behavioral differences on fingerprinted versus fingerprint-free versions of the same test image.
why_important: Synthetic data is becoming core training infrastructure; if gains are partly artifact-coupled, they will not transfer to real-world deployment and will break when generator versions change, an unmeasured fragility in current practice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: generator fingerprints are known in forensics; their role as shortcut features in segmentation training gains appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models on original and fingerprint-suppressed synthetic augmentation sets and compare gains on real test data plus fingerprint-sensitivity probes.
main_risk: Fingerprint suppression may also remove genuine high-frequency content; suppression quality must be validated with both detectors and quality metrics.
default_community_belief: Synthetic-data gains reflect content diversity and label quality, transferring fully to real-world inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Heavy training augmentation (resizing, compression) may already destroy fingerprints, meaning gains were content-driven all along.
fastest_falsification: Fingerprint-sensitivity probe on an existing synthetic-augmented model (evaluate on spectrally filtered test copies), hours.

one_line: Self-consuming training loops for segmentation collapse boundary complexity before class statistics shift, providing an early-warning metric generations before visible model collapse.
problem: Iterated training on model-generated images and pseudo-labels is known to degrade generative models, but which segmentation-relevant statistics degrade first, and how to detect the process early, is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Boundary geometry is the least constrained, highest-entropy component of mask distributions, so generational recycling smooths and regularizes boundaries first; boundary complexity measures (curvature spectra, fractal-dimension proxies) will decay generations before class balance, object counts, or aggregate accuracy show drift.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled self-consuming loops, boundary-complexity statistics of generated masks will show significant monotone decay by the second or third generation while class frequencies and mIoU on real data remain within noise, and the decay rate will predict later aggregate collapse timing.
why_important: As synthetic recycling becomes unavoidable at web scale, early-warning indicators determine whether the community can monitor and mitigate quality decay; a leading indicator grounded in which statistics are least anchored is both practical and theoretically informative.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: model collapse is studied for distributions broadly; a segmentation-specific leading-indicator analysis based on boundary entropy appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a compact self-consuming loop (generator plus segmenter pseudo-labeling) for several generations, tracking boundary-complexity metrics against class statistics and real-data accuracy.
main_risk: Loop design choices (mixing ratios of real data) strongly affect decay dynamics; conclusions must be mapped across mixing ratios to be useful.
default_community_belief: Model collapse manifests as visible quality and diversity loss detectable by standard metrics when it matters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-frequency drift might actually lead boundary smoothing in mask-space recycling, inverting the proposed indicator ordering.
fastest_falsification: Two-generation loop at small scale with boundary-statistics tracking, a few days of compute.

one_line: Synthetic scenes have systematically simpler occlusion topology than reality, and occlusion complexity is the variable that predicts where synthetically pretrained segmenters fail on real data.
problem: The synthetic-to-real gap is attributed to appearance realism, driving investment in photorealism, while structural scene statistics like occlusion layering go unmeasured and unmatched.
core_hypothesis: Generated and simulated scenes exhibit fewer occlusion layers, simpler junction structure, and less fragmented visibility than real scenes; models pretrained on them underperform specifically on high-occlusion-complexity real images, and matching occlusion statistics closes more of the gap than improving texture realism.
falsifiable_prediction: Occlusion-complexity histograms of popular synthetic segmentation datasets will differ significantly from real benchmarks; real-image error of synthetically pretrained models will correlate with per-image occlusion complexity after content controls, and occlusion-matched synthetic data will beat photorealism-matched data at equal volume.
why_important: It redirects synthetic-data engineering from expensive photorealism to a measurable structural target, and provides a per-image predictor of where synthetic-trained models should not be trusted.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: domain gap analyses emphasize appearance; occlusion-topology statistics as the dominant structural gap variable appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute occlusion-complexity statistics for one synthetic and one real dataset from available depth or amodal annotations, correlate synthetic-pretrained model errors with per-image complexity, and run a small occlusion-matched generation study.
main_risk: Measuring occlusion complexity on real data needs amodal or depth annotations, limiting dataset choice; proxies from panoptic structure must be validated first.
default_community_belief: Closing the appearance gap (photorealism) is the main route to making synthetic data effective for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance and occlusion complexity may be confounded in current generators such that improving one improves the other, making the dissociation hard to demonstrate.
fastest_falsification: Occlusion-statistics comparison between one synthetic and one real dataset, one day.

one_line: Co-generated image-mask training pairs align too perfectly: models trained on them acquire unrealistic boundary-precision expectations that degrade performance on human-annotated reality.
problem: Generative pipelines that produce images and masks jointly deliver pixel-perfect correspondence, unlike human annotation which carries systematic imprecision; the effect of training on impossibly clean alignment is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on perfectly aligned synthetic pairs learn sharp, high-confidence boundary transitions calibrated to zero annotation noise; on real data with annotator imprecision, this manifests as brittle boundary behavior and metric loss relative to models trained with alignment noise matched to human statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: Injecting empirically calibrated annotation-noise models into synthetic masks during training will improve real-data boundary metrics over clean-mask training at equal data volume, and the improvement will scale with the match between injected and target-dataset annotator-noise statistics.
why_important: It inverts a core assumption of synthetic data (cleaner labels are better) with a testable mechanism, implying synthetic pipelines should model annotation imperfection as part of the label distribution rather than eliminating it.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: label-noise robustness is studied as a defense; deliberately matching synthetic label noise to human annotator statistics as an alignment-realism method appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate annotator-noise statistics from a multi-rater subset, train models on synthetic pairs with and without matched noise injection, and compare real-data boundary metrics.
main_risk: Gains may be confounded with generic regularization from label smoothing; matched-entropy random-noise controls are required.
default_community_belief: Perfect synthetic label alignment is an advantage of generated data over human annotation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loss functions may already absorb the alignment mismatch, making noise matching redundant with standard training tricks.
fastest_falsification: Clean versus noise-matched synthetic training at small scale on one dataset, two days.

one_line: Copy-paste and diffusion-inpainting augmentation teach opposite lessons: one builds boundary-artifact robustness, the other builds context-object binding that fails under context shift.
problem: Both augmentation families report gains on in-distribution benchmarks, so they are treated as interchangeable synthetic-data strategies, without asking what invariances each installs.
core_hypothesis: Copy-paste creates context-implausible compositions, forcing context-independent object recognition; inpainting generates context-consistent objects, reinforcing context-object co-occurrence priors; the two therefore produce opposite behavior on out-of-context test sets while looking equivalent in-distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched in-distribution gains, copy-paste-trained models will significantly outperform inpainting-augmented models on out-of-context object benchmarks, while inpainting-augmented models will win on context-consistent scenes, a crossover interaction robust across backbones.
why_important: Augmentation choice silently determines context reliance, a first-order deployment property for open-world systems; the crossover, if real, gives practitioners a principled selection rule instead of leaderboard mimicry.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: both methods are studied separately; a controlled contrast on the context-dependence axis with crossover prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with each augmentation on one dataset, evaluate on context-consistent and out-of-context test splits, and test the interaction term.
main_risk: Out-of-context benchmarks are small and idiosyncratic; constructing a fair context-shift evaluation is the main methodological burden.
default_community_belief: Synthetic augmentation methods differ in realism and effort but push models in broadly the same beneficial direction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern large backbones may already encode context-robust recognition, leaving no room for augmentation to change context reliance either way.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate existing copy-paste-trained and inpainting-augmented checkpoints on an out-of-context test set, one day.

one_line: Invisible watermarks embedded in synthetic training images become learned features, coupling segmentation models to watermark schemes that will change under them.
problem: Generated images increasingly carry imperceptible provenance watermarks by policy; synthetic-data pipelines feed these watermarked images into training without considering the watermark as a learnable signal.
core_hypothesis: Watermark patterns are consistent, low-level, and correlated with the synthetic subset's label statistics, so models learn watermark-conditional processing; performance will shift measurably when the same content is presented with a different or absent watermark, and watermark-scheme updates by generator vendors will silently change model behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with watermarked synthetic data will show statistically significant output differences on identical images with watermarks re-encoded or stripped, exceeding perturbation-energy-matched controls, while models trained on watermark-free synthetic data will not.
why_important: It identifies an infrastructure-level fragility: model behavior tied to a third party's watermarking scheme, which can change without notice, is an unacknowledged supply-chain dependency of synthetic-data training.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: watermark robustness is studied from the forensics side; the reverse question of watermarks as learned features in downstream dense-prediction training appears unasked.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models on watermarked and watermark-stripped synthetic sets, then compare sensitivity to watermark presence on identical test content.
main_risk: Watermark stripping tools imperfectly remove signals; residual watermark energy must be quantified to interpret negative results.
default_community_belief: Imperceptible watermarks are semantically inert and cannot influence trained model behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Watermark energy may sit in frequency bands that standard augmentation destroys, making the learned dependence negligible in realistic pipelines.
fastest_falsification: Watermark-presence sensitivity probe on an existing synthetic-trained model, hours.

one_line: The real-image supply is drifting: web photographs are increasingly SR-processed and AI-enhanced before upload, so datasets of the future inherit restoration priors in their supposedly natural images.
problem: Device pipelines now apply on-board SR, denoising, and generative enhancement by default; dataset builders treat scraped photos as natural signal, ignoring that the population of available images is shifting toward restoration-processed statistics.
core_hypothesis: The fraction of scraped images bearing measurable enhancement fingerprints is rising over upload year; models trained on recent scrapes internalize enhancement statistics as the definition of natural, degrading relative performance on unprocessed sensor data (scientific, industrial, archival) in a measurable, growing way.
falsifiable_prediction: Enhancement-fingerprint detectors will show a monotone increase in processed-image fraction as a function of image upload year in public collections, and segmentation models trained on recent-year subsets will underperform earlier-year-trained counterparts specifically on raw unprocessed imagery at matched content.
why_important: It documents a slow corruption of the field's raw material: the concept of a natural image is becoming device-generation-dependent, which affects every claim about learning from real data and argues for provenance-stratified dataset curation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: individual device enhancements are documented; a longitudinal population-drift analysis linked to downstream segmentation consequences appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run enhancement-fingerprint analysis over upload-year-stratified samples of a large public image collection and train year-stratified models evaluated on raw sensor benchmarks.
main_risk: Upload-year metadata is noisy and confounded with content and camera-population changes; camera-model controls are needed for the trend claim.
default_community_belief: Scraped photographs are natural images; enhancement processing is an edge case rather than a population-level trend.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fingerprints of diverse proprietary enhancement pipelines may be too heterogeneous to detect reliably, making the trend unmeasurable even if real.
fastest_falsification: Fingerprint-rate comparison between old and recent upload-year samples of one collection, two days.

one_line: Segmentation models are systematically more accurate on generated images than on real ones at matched apparent difficulty, making the accuracy gap itself a contamination detector.
problem: There is no cheap tool to flag synthetic admixture in evaluation sets; detection relies on forensic classifiers that generalize poorly across generators.
core_hypothesis: Generated images are prior-conformant (canonical poses, clean boundaries, typical layouts) in ways that align with what segmentation models learned, so per-image accuracy is higher on synthetic content even when human-judged difficulty is matched; the accuracy differential generalizes across generator families better than forensic features do.
falsifiable_prediction: On mixed sets with known provenance, per-image segmentation quality scores will separate real from generated images with useful discrimination after controlling for content and difficulty, and this separation will transfer to a held-out generator family better than a forensic classifier trained on the same provenance labels.
why_important: A task-behavioral contamination signal that survives generator updates would give benchmark maintainers a sustainable auditing tool, and its existence would itself demonstrate the prior-conformance of synthetic imagery in task-relevant respects.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: forensic detection is a large field; using downstream task performance differentials as a provenance signal appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble real and generated image sets with segmentation labels, match difficulty via human ratings or proxy statistics, and compare per-image accuracy distributions plus cross-generator transfer of the resulting detector.
main_risk: Labels for generated images must come from the generation process or annotation, and annotation on synthetic images may itself be easier, confounding the comparison; annotation-protocol controls are needed.
default_community_belief: Model accuracy depends on image difficulty and content, not on whether the image is real or generated per se.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Difficulty matching may be impossible to do convincingly, since ease-for-models may be exactly what defines generated images, collapsing the claim into circularity.
fastest_falsification: Accuracy-differential measurement on an existing mixed-provenance set, one day.

one_line: Generative augmentation can leak test sets through memorization: models trained on diffusion outputs inherit near-duplicates of the generator's training images, including benchmark test images.
problem: Teams augment training data with outputs from generators whose own training corpora are undocumented and likely include public benchmark images; the resulting indirect contamination path is unaudited.
core_hypothesis: Diffusion models regurgitate near-copies of training images at low but nonzero rates; when benchmark test images were in the generator's corpus, augmentation samples will include recognizable near-duplicates, giving augmented models illegitimate exposure to test content and inflating scores through a path invisible to standard dedup checks against the training set.
falsifiable_prediction: Perceptual-hash and embedding-based retrieval will find near-duplicates of benchmark test images inside large generated augmentation pools at rates above chance matching, and augmented models will show anomalously high accuracy precisely on the matched test images relative to unmatched ones.
why_important: It extends the contamination frontier from datasets to generators: benchmark integrity now depends on the training corpora of third-party models, requiring generation-aware dedup protocols before synthetic augmentation results can be trusted.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: memorization in diffusion models is established; the specific chain into segmentation benchmark inflation with per-image accuracy verification appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate a large augmentation pool with a public model, retrieve near-duplicates of one benchmark's test set, and compare per-image test accuracy of an augmented model on matched versus unmatched test images.
main_risk: Near-duplicate rates may be too low for statistical power at feasible generation volumes; power analysis should precede the main experiment.
default_community_belief: Deduplicating one's own training data against the test set guarantees contamination-free evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmark test images may be rare in generator corpora or protected by dedup at the generator-training stage, making the leak path negligible in practice.
fastest_falsification: Retrieval of test-set near-duplicates in an existing public generated-image pool, one day.

one_line: Self-supervised microscopy denoisers delete dim puncta by design, biasing count-based biology downward in proportion to structure sparsity.
problem: Noise2X-style self-supervised denoisers are standard in fluorescence microscopy pipelines feeding puncta segmentation and counting, but their treatment of signals statistically indistinguishable from noise at single-pixel scale is not audited against biological quantification.
core_hypothesis: Self-supervised denoising objectives cannot distinguish sparse dim puncta from noise spikes without spatial-context priors that dim isolated puncta lack; denoisers therefore suppress them systematically, and downstream puncta counts are biased downward with the bias growing as puncta get dimmer and sparser.
falsifiable_prediction: On semi-synthetic data (real noise plus inserted puncta of controlled intensity and density), denoised-then-segmented counts will underestimate truth increasingly as intensity drops and sparsity rises, while raw-image segmentation with matched training will show smaller, unbiased errors at the same operating points.
why_important: Synapse, vesicle, and molecule counting drive biological conclusions; a preprocessing-induced downward bias correlated with signal dimness would systematically distort dose-response and comparison studies that pass all standard image-quality checks.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: denoiser hallucination is discussed qualitatively in microscopy; a quantitative count-bias law versus intensity and sparsity for self-supervised denoisers appears unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert calibrated puncta into real dark-frame noise, run two self-supervised denoisers, segment, and map count bias over the intensity-density grid.
main_risk: Insertion realism (PSF, camera gain) must be validated against real single-molecule data or the bias map will not transfer to practice.
default_community_belief: Self-supervised denoising is a safe default that improves all downstream microscopy quantification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: PSF-scale spatial correlation of true puncta may be sufficient context for denoisers to preserve them, keeping the bias negligible above single-pixel signals.
fastest_falsification: Puncta-insertion bias measurement with one public microscopy denoiser, one day.

one_line: Stain normalization is restoration in disguise: it hallucinates tissue chemistry, and borderline cells flip diagnostic class depending on which normalization method prepared the slide.
problem: Stain normalization is applied as neutral preprocessing in computational pathology, but it re-estimates stain concentrations from appearance, which is an inverse problem with prior-dependent solutions.
core_hypothesis: Different normalization methods resolve stain-ambiguity differently, so cells near class decision boundaries (weakly stained, mixed morphology) receive systematically different downstream labels per method; the flip population is not random but concentrated in diagnostically ambiguous cells, where it matters most.
falsifiable_prediction: Running one frozen cell-classification or segmentation model on the same WSIs normalized by three methods will show label flips concentrated on cells with intermediate stain statistics, at rates significantly above matched controls, and flip direction will be method-specific and reproducible.
why_important: Normalization choice is unreported in most pathology AI studies; if it selectively relabels ambiguous cells, cross-study performance differences and site-transfer results are partly normalization artifacts with direct clinical relevance.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: normalization methods are compared by downstream accuracy; a flip-population analysis showing concentration on diagnostically borderline cells appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Normalize one annotated WSI set with three methods, run a frozen model, characterize the flip population against stain-statistic and morphology covariates.
main_risk: Ground truth for borderline cells is itself uncertain; multi-pathologist reference labels on the flip population are needed to interpret flips as errors versus legitimate ambiguity.
default_community_belief: Stain normalization removes nuisance variation without affecting the biological content models read.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models trained with stain augmentation may be normalization-invariant, making flips rare regardless of method.
fastest_falsification: Three-method flip-rate analysis on one public pathology dataset, one day.

one_line: Gigapixel WSI stitching seams create phantom boundaries that segmentation models learn to avoid, and benchmark scores are inflated because annotations systematically exclude seam regions.
problem: Whole-slide images are assembled from scanned tiles with blending seams; neither model behavior at seams nor the spatial distribution of annotations relative to seams has been audited.
core_hypothesis: Seam artifacts act as spurious edges that models trained on WSI data learn to treat specially (avoiding or snapping to them), and annotators preferentially annotate away from visually disrupted seam areas, so reported accuracy overestimates true whole-slide performance in a seam-position-predictable way.
falsifiable_prediction: Error rates of published WSI segmentation models will be significantly elevated within a measurable band around scanner seam positions, and annotation-density maps will show significant depletion in the same bands, jointly implying benchmark inflation proportional to seam-band area fraction.
why_important: Clinical WSI analysis processes entire slides including seams; a seam-localized error band invisible to benchmarks means deployed sensitivity is lower than reported, particularly for small lesions that can fall on seams.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: stitching artifacts are known to scanner engineers; a quantitative seam-stratified error and annotation-density analysis for segmentation benchmarks appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recover seam positions from scanner metadata or artifact detection on one WSI benchmark, compute seam-band error and annotation density for a public model, and estimate the inflation correction.
main_risk: Seam positions may be unrecoverable for some scanner formats, restricting the study to scanners with documented tiling geometry.
default_community_belief: WSI stitching is engineering-grade seamless and irrelevant to model evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern scanners with high-overlap blending may produce seams too weak to influence either models or annotators.
fastest_falsification: Seam-band error analysis on one benchmark with recoverable tiling geometry, two days.

one_line: A large share of hard cases in pathology segmentation benchmarks are focus artifacts, not difficult biology: local focus score predicts error better than any semantic variable.
problem: Failure analyses in computational pathology explain errors with biological difficulty (rare morphologies, ambiguous lesions), while per-region optical focus quality, which varies strongly across WSIs, is rarely included as a covariate.
core_hypothesis: Scanner autofocus errors create locally blurred regions whose degraded evidence, not biology, drives a large fraction of segmentation failures; local focus metrics will dominate semantic covariates in explaining error variance, and restoring or excluding defocused regions will resolve much of the presumed hard-case population.
falsifiable_prediction: Regression of per-region segmentation error on focus scores plus semantic covariates will attribute a dominant share of explainable variance to focus, and deblurring-based reprocessing of defocused regions will convert a large fraction of hard cases to correct predictions without any model change.
why_important: Misattributing focus artifacts to biological difficulty steers research toward better models when the fix is better acquisition QC or targeted restoration, and it corrupts hard-case-mining pipelines that are supposed to surface genuinely difficult biology.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: focus QC exists as an acquisition step; its quantified role as the dominant hard-case generator in segmentation benchmarks appears undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute focus maps on one benchmark, regress errors on focus and semantic covariates, and reprocess the defocused hard cases with deblurring to measure conversion rates.
main_risk: Focus and biology may correlate (thick lesions defocus more), requiring careful causal interpretation and possibly refocused rescans of a subset.
default_community_belief: Benchmark hard cases represent biologically or morphologically difficult content that better models should solve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In well-curated benchmarks, QC may have already removed defocused regions, leaving biology as the genuine driver.
fastest_falsification: Focus-error correlation on one public WSI benchmark, one day.

one_line: Computational super-resolution microscopy reconstructions impose continuity priors that fabricate filament connections, making a fraction of downstream cytoskeleton topology algorithmic artifact.
problem: SMLM and SIM reconstructions solve severely ill-posed inverse problems with regularizers favoring smooth continuous structures, and downstream network-topology analysis treats the reconstructions as observations.
core_hypothesis: Continuity-favoring regularization bridges sub-resolution gaps between distinct filaments, so segmentation-derived topology (junction counts, connectivity) contains reconstruction-parameter-dependent false connections; varying reconstruction hyperparameters on identical raw data will change topology conclusions beyond biological plausibility.
falsifiable_prediction: Reconstructing the same raw SMLM/SIM acquisitions under a hyperparameter sweep will produce topology metrics whose variance across settings is comparable to or exceeds reported biological effect sizes in the cytoskeleton literature, and gap-bridging events will localize at sub-resolution inter-filament distances.
why_important: If topology claims depend on reconstruction settings, a class of published biological conclusions inherits an unquantified algorithmic degree of freedom, and reporting standards need reconstruction-sensitivity analyses the way statistics require robustness checks.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: reconstruction artifacts are studied for resolution claims; propagating hyperparameter sensitivity into downstream segmentation-topology conclusions appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public raw super-resolution microscopy data, sweep reconstruction parameters, segment filaments, and quantify topology-metric dispersion against published biological effect sizes.
main_risk: Ground-truth topology is unavailable for real data; simulated filament phantoms with realistic photophysics are needed to anchor which settings are closest to truth.
default_community_belief: Validated reconstruction algorithms yield structures faithful enough that downstream topology reflects biology.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Topology metrics may be robust to the realistic hyperparameter range even if pixel-level outputs differ, leaving biological conclusions intact.
fastest_falsification: Two-setting reconstruction comparison with topology extraction on one public dataset, two days.

one_line: Scanner-side JPEG2000 compression degrades diagnostic chromatin texture before stromal texture, making nuclei-subtype segmentation compression-fragile in a predictable order.
problem: WSIs are stored with lossy compression configured for visual acceptability; which biological structures lose machine-usable information first as compression tightens is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: Fine chromatin patterns that discriminate nuclei subtypes occupy the high-frequency bands compression discards first, while coarse stromal architecture survives; subtype segmentation accuracy will therefore collapse in a predictable class order as bitrate decreases, long before pathologists judge the images degraded.
falsifiable_prediction: Recompressing raw or lightly compressed WSIs across bitrates will show per-class accuracy collapse orderings consistent with each class's discriminative-frequency profile, with chromatin-dependent subtypes failing at bitrates rated visually acceptable in reader studies.
why_important: Storage policies are set institution-wide by visual criteria; demonstrating machine-diagnostic loss at visually acceptable compression forces bitrate standards to be task-referenced, affecting archives feeding future AI training and validation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compression effects on pathology AI are studied in aggregate; a class-ordered collapse law tied to discriminative-frequency profiles appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bitrate sweep on one annotated WSI set, per-class accuracy curves, and comparison of collapse order with pre-computed class frequency profiles.
main_risk: Access to uncompressed or losslessly stored WSIs is limited; conclusions from already-compressed sources underestimate true sensitivity.
default_community_belief: Standard scanner compression settings are safely above the threshold where machine analysis is affected.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may rely on mid-frequency morphology more than fine chromatin texture, keeping subtype accuracy stable deep into compression.
fastest_falsification: Recompression accuracy sweep on one public dataset, one day.

one_line: Pathology models entangle two size signals: microns-per-pixel metadata errors reveal whether models read absolute cell size as diagnostic signal or as scanner shortcut.
problem: Cell size is genuinely diagnostic, but effective magnification varies across scanners and metadata errors are common; models may encode size via pixel measurements tied to scanner identity rather than physical calibration, and the two are never dissociated.
core_hypothesis: Models trained across scanners without explicit physical-size normalization learn scanner-conditional size expectations; controlled rescaling experiments will show prediction shifts tracking pixel size rather than physical size, meaning size is being read as a shortcut vulnerable to magnification and metadata drift.
falsifiable_prediction: Synthetically rescaling test images while updating or withholding MPP metadata will shift predictions of cross-scanner-trained models in the direction of pixel-size expectations, and per-site errors in the wild will correlate with each site's deviation from the training-population MPP distribution.
why_important: Magnification heterogeneity is universal in multi-site pathology; if size reading is pixel-referenced, silent metadata errors change diagnoses, and harmonization must enforce physical-unit normalization rather than trusting learned invariance.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: scanner domain shift is studied via color and texture; a controlled dissociation of physical-size signal from pixel-size shortcut appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rescaling sweep with metadata manipulation on one multi-scanner dataset and a frozen model, measuring prediction drift against physical-size ground truth from calibrated slides.
main_risk: Rescaling introduces interpolation artifacts that must be controlled with matched-resampling baselines to avoid confounding the size effect.
default_community_belief: Multi-scanner training teaches models scale invariance sufficient for cross-site deployment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong scale augmentation in modern pipelines may have already broken pixel-size reliance, leaving only genuine physical-size sensitivity.
fastest_falsification: Rescaling-drift measurement on one public multi-scanner model, hours.

one_line: Natural-image diffusion priors impose reflected-light shading physics on transmitted-light microscopy, producing plausible-but-wrong intensity structure that biases confluence and density estimates.
problem: Generic diffusion restorers are increasingly applied to microscopy for denoising and enhancement, but their priors encode photographic illumination (shadows, specular highlights, vignetting semantics) that transmitted-light physics does not produce.
core_hypothesis: When evidence is weak, natural-image-pretrained restorers introduce shading gradients and edge lighting consistent with reflected-light scenes; in brightfield or phase imaging this fabricates intensity structure that downstream cell segmentation reads as confluence or density variation, biasing culture-level quantification.
falsifiable_prediction: Restoring paired degraded brightfield images with natural-image diffusion models will introduce spatially coherent low-frequency intensity deviations absent from microscopy-trained restorer outputs, and confluence estimates from segmentation will shift systematically in the natural-prior arm relative to ground truth.
why_important: Cross-domain reuse of foundation restorers is the default economic choice; a physics-mismatch bias measurable at the assay level (confluence, growth curves) directly affects experimental conclusions in routine cell biology workflows.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: domain mismatch for restorers is generic knowledge; identifying illumination-physics transfer as the specific mechanism with assay-level consequences appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare paired restorations from natural-image and microscopy-trained diffusion models on degraded brightfield data, decompose deviations into low-frequency shading components, and measure downstream confluence bias.
main_risk: Microscopy-trained restorers of comparable capacity may not exist publicly, requiring training a control model to make the comparison fair.
default_community_belief: Foundation restorers transfer to microscopy with at worst generic quality loss, not with structured physical bias.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong conditioning on the degraded input may pin low-frequency structure, confining prior mismatch to high-frequency texture where assay impact is negligible.
fastest_falsification: Shading-component analysis of natural-prior restorations on public brightfield data, one day.

one_line: Microscopy ground truth is drawn on deconvolved or contrast-stretched views, so models trained on raw frames chase boundaries that exist only in the enhanced rendering, with a recoverable constant offset.
problem: Annotation interfaces for microscopy apply default enhancement (deconvolution previews, auto-contrast) that alters apparent structure extents, while training consumes raw or differently processed pixels; the render-train mismatch is undocumented in most datasets.
core_hypothesis: Enhancement systematically shifts apparent boundaries (deconvolution shrinks blurred halos, contrast stretch moves threshold crossings), so labels carry a rendering-specific boundary convention; models trained on raw images exhibit a consistent signed boundary offset equal to the render-raw discrepancy, which re-rendering the training images can remove.
falsifiable_prediction: For datasets whose annotation-rendering pipeline can be reconstructed, the average signed boundary error of raw-trained models will match the independently measured render-raw boundary displacement in magnitude and direction, and training on re-rendered images will remove that error component.
why_important: A constant recoverable bias masquerading as model error inflates the apparent difficulty of microscopy segmentation and corrupts cross-dataset comparisons where rendering conventions differ; the fix is procedural, not architectural.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotation-protocol effects are acknowledged qualitatively; a quantitative render-offset accounting with removal-by-re-rendering validation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reconstruct the annotation rendering for one dataset, measure render-raw boundary displacement on calibration structures, and compare with the signed error of a raw-trained model before and after re-rendered training.
main_risk: Annotation-rendering metadata is often lost, limiting candidate datasets; the study may need to generate a purpose-built dual-rendered annotation set.
default_community_belief: Label error is annotator noise; the rendering shown during annotation is not tracked as a bias source.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may compensate mentally for rendering effects using domain expertise, leaving offsets far smaller than the physical rendering displacement.
fastest_falsification: Render-raw displacement measurement on calibration beads plus model signed-error comparison, two days.

one_line: Patch-based WSI segmentation has a measurable context ceiling: pathologists' region boundaries depend on gigapixel-scale architecture that no patch-level model can access.
problem: WSI pipelines process fixed-size patches for memory reasons, assuming local evidence suffices; how much boundary placement in expert annotation depends on slide-level context has not been quantified as an information ceiling.
core_hypothesis: Expert boundaries for architectural entities (tumor regions, growth patterns) integrate spatial context far beyond patch scale; annotator consistency measured at patch view versus region view will quantify a context information gap that upper-bounds any patch-level model, explaining a fixed residual gap that model scaling cannot close.
falsifiable_prediction: Experts re-annotating from isolated patches will disagree with their own slide-level annotations substantially more than intra-view repeat annotation, and patch-level model errors will concentrate exactly where the expert patch-view versus slide-view disagreement is highest.
why_important: It converts an architecture debate (bigger context windows for WSI) into a measured information requirement, telling the field how much accuracy is structurally unreachable at each context size and where multi-scale context is genuinely necessary rather than fashionable.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: context aggregation methods exist; an annotator-based information-ceiling measurement for WSI segmentation appears not to have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-view re-annotation study with two or three pathologists on one dataset, plus co-localization analysis of patch-model errors with view-disagreement maps.
main_risk: Expert time is expensive and intra-annotator drift between sessions must be separated from the view effect with proper counterbalancing.
default_community_belief: Patch-level evidence is adequate for segmentation, and residual errors reflect model rather than information limitations.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For many tissue classes local texture may fully determine labels, making the context ceiling relevant only to a minority of architectural boundaries.
fastest_falsification: Small pilot with one pathologist re-annotating 50 patches from their own slide-level work, days including recruitment.

one_line: Denoising-enabled low-light live-cell imaging changes the biology it measures: residual restoration bias correlates with motion, distorting motility statistics.
problem: Restoration is marketed as enabling gentler imaging (less phototoxicity) with equal analysis quality, but restoration errors on moving objects are structured, and motility analysis consumes exactly the moving content.
core_hypothesis: Denoisers exploit temporal context in which movement violates their implicit stationarity assumptions, so restoration error is motion-correlated; segmentation-derived tracks from denoised low-light acquisitions will show biased speed and shape-change statistics relative to matched high-light ground truth, in directions predictable from the denoiser's temporal window.
falsifiable_prediction: Paired high-light and denoised low-light acquisitions of the same cultures will yield motility distributions that differ significantly, with bias magnitude increasing with cell speed and with the denoiser's temporal aggregation length, while static-morphology statistics stay matched.
why_important: Phototoxicity-reduction protocols justified by image-quality parity may alter the biological measurements they were adopted to protect; a motion-correlated bias undermines low-light live-cell studies precisely for dynamics, their main purpose.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: restoration quality for live imaging is validated on static metrics; assay-level motility bias from temporal denoising appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Acquire or reuse paired-illumination live-cell data, run temporal denoisers with different window lengths, and compare track-level motility statistics against the high-light reference.
main_risk: Truly paired acquisitions are hard because illumination itself may change behavior; interleaved-frame designs are needed to control biology.
default_community_belief: If restored low-light images match high-light images on quality metrics, analyses performed on them are equivalent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern flow-aware denoisers may handle motion well enough that residual motility bias is below biological effect sizes of interest.
fastest_falsification: Track-statistic comparison on one public paired or interleaved dataset, two days.

one_line: Learned axial super-resolution in volumetric microscopy fabricates 3D morphology: isotropy-restored volumes bias shape metrics like sphericity in a consistent, quantifiable direction.
problem: Axial resolution is physically worse than lateral in most volumetric microscopy, and learned isotropic restoration is used before 3D segmentation and morphometry, without auditing what the fabricated axial detail does to shape statistics.
core_hypothesis: Isotropy networks learn lateral-statistics priors and impose them axially, regularizing elongated or irregular axial structure toward laterally typical shapes; 3D morphology metrics computed after restoration are therefore biased toward compactness, with the bias direction stable across models trained on similar data.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic phantoms with known 3D shapes imaged under realistic anisotropic PSFs, restored-then-segmented morphology will show systematic sphericity inflation and axial-extent shrinkage relative to truth, exceeding the bias of classical interpolation baselines at matched apparent quality.
why_important: 3D morphometry supports claims about cell state and tissue organization; a preprocessing-induced compactness bias would systematically distort such claims while making images look better, the worst combination for scientific reliability.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: isotropic restoration is evaluated by image similarity; propagation into morphometric bias with phantom-based direction estimates appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate anisotropic acquisition of known phantoms, apply learned isotropy restoration and interpolation baselines, segment, and compare shape-metric bias distributions.
main_risk: Phantom realism (texture, noise, PSF accuracy) determines transferability; validation against a small real dataset with orthogonal-view ground truth is needed.
default_community_belief: Learned isotropic restoration recovers axial structure faithfully enough for downstream quantitative analysis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For structures within the training distribution, fabricated axial detail may be statistically accurate, keeping morphometric bias negligible in practice.
fastest_falsification: Phantom-based sphericity bias measurement with one public isotropy model, two days.

one_line: Virtual staining is segmentation laundering: evaluating segmentation on virtually stained images double-counts the staining model's prior and reports information the input never contained.
problem: Virtual staining (label-free to fluorescence prediction) followed by segmentation is an increasingly common pipeline, evaluated by segmentation accuracy on the virtual stain as if the stain were observed data.
core_hypothesis: The staining network already solves much of the segmentation problem internally, painting class-defining contrast where its prior expects structures; downstream segmentation then reads back the prior, so reported accuracy exceeds the information actually extractable from the label-free input, especially where the prior happens to match ground truth by typicality rather than evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: Input-ablation tests (masking or perturbing label-free evidence in regions and measuring virtual-stain persistence) will show stain structure persisting without supporting input evidence, and segmentation accuracy on virtual stains will exceed accuracy of models trained directly on label-free inputs by a margin that shrinks toward zero on atypical structures where priors fail.
why_important: If virtual-stain pipelines report prior-conformance as measurement, biological findings on atypical or diseased samples (where priors mismatch) inherit invisible failure, and pipeline validation needs information-flow accounting rather than endpoint accuracy alone.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: virtual staining papers validate against real stains in aggregate; an information-accounting critique with evidence-ablation methodology appears not standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or obtain one virtual-staining model, run evidence-ablation persistence tests, and compare direct label-free segmentation against stain-then-segment on typical versus atypical structure subsets.
main_risk: Ablations must respect input statistics to avoid trivially detectable perturbations that the network treats as artifacts rather than absence of evidence.
default_community_belief: Good agreement of virtual stains with real stains validates the pipeline for downstream quantitative use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Label-free contrast may genuinely contain most of the needed information, making the prior contribution small and the laundering critique moot for common assays.
fastest_falsification: Evidence-ablation persistence test on a public virtual-staining model, one day.

one_line: WSI foundation-model embeddings encode scanner identity more strongly than tissue class at shallow depths, and restoration-style harmonization removes diagnostic signal along with the scanner signal.
problem: Pathology foundation models are adopted for cross-site deployment, with scanner effects assumed to wash out during large-scale pretraining; the layer-wise geometry of scanner versus biology information, and the cost of removing scanner information, are unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Scanner identity is linearly decodable from shallow and mid-level embeddings at higher accuracy than tissue class, explaining cross-site transfer failures; harmonization methods that suppress scanner-predictive components (image-space restoration or embedding projection) also remove a measurable share of diagnostically relevant variance, creating an unavoidable tradeoff that should be reported per method.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise probing of public pathology foundation models will show scanner decodability exceeding tissue-class decodability in early layers; applying scanner-removal harmonization will degrade tissue-class probe accuracy by a nonzero, method-dependent amount, and the harmonization-tradeoff curve will predict cross-site segmentation transfer performance.
why_important: The field currently frames harmonization as free noise removal; a quantified biology-cost per unit of scanner-signal removal changes how site generalization should be engineered and reported, especially for regulatory validation of pathology AI.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: batch effects are known in pathology; a layer-wise decodability comparison with a harmonization tradeoff curve linked to segmentation transfer appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe scanner and tissue decodability across layers of one public pathology foundation model on a multi-scanner dataset, apply two harmonization methods, and measure the biology-cost and transfer-prediction claims.
main_risk: Scanner and site confound with case mix; tissue-matched multi-scanner data (same blocks scanned on multiple devices) is the clean substrate and is scarce.
default_community_belief: Foundation-scale pretraining largely solves scanner variation, and harmonization is a lossless cleanup step.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scanner decodability may reflect harmless nuisance dimensions orthogonal to diagnostic features, in which case harmonization costs nothing and transfer failures have other causes.
fastest_falsification: Layer-wise scanner-versus-tissue probing on one public model and multi-scanner dataset, one day.

one_line: Video segmentation accuracy oscillates with codec GOP structure: masks are measurably better on I-frames than on B-frames, creating a periodic artifact no shuffled-frame evaluation can see.
problem: Video models are evaluated on frames sampled without regard to codec frame type, though compression quality differs systematically between intra-coded and bidirectionally predicted frames.
core_hypothesis: B-frames carry motion-compensated residual artifacts and lower effective bitrate, so per-frame segmentation quality is periodic and phase-locked to GOP structure; streaming systems consuming compressed video inherit a rhythmic accuracy modulation that aliases into downstream temporal analytics.
falsifiable_prediction: Frame-type-stratified evaluation on compressed benchmarks will show consistent I-frame accuracy exceeding B-frame accuracy at fixed content (measured via frame-type-aligned re-encoding of the same clips), with the gap growing as bitrate decreases and vanishing on losslessly stored video.
why_important: Millions of deployed pipelines analyze compressed streams; a codec-phase-locked accuracy signal biases event detection timing and any metric aggregated without frame-type balance, and it is invisible to standard random-frame evaluation protocols.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compression robustness is studied at clip level; frame-type-resolved segmentation accuracy analysis with phase-locking demonstration appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-encode one video benchmark at several bitrates, evaluate a frozen video segmenter with frame-type labels from the bitstream, and test the periodic accuracy structure.
main_risk: Frame-type effects may be confounded with motion (B-frames cluster in high-motion spans); re-encoding the same frames under shifted GOP phase controls for content.
default_community_belief: Compression affects video analysis through average quality; frame-level codec structure is below the level models notice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal-propagation models may smooth over per-frame quality differences, flattening the oscillation that per-frame models would show.
fastest_falsification: Frame-type-stratified evaluation on one compressed benchmark, hours.

one_line: Video segmentation models trained on compressed footage exploit codec artifacts as motion cues, so they degrade on raw or differently encoded video: a reverse domain gap.
problem: Training corpora for video models are almost exclusively compressed web video, and motion-related codec artifacts (blocking along motion boundaries, residual pulsing) correlate with the very quantities models need to estimate.
core_hypothesis: Models learn to read codec-induced motion signatures as features; on uncompressed or novel-codec footage these cues vanish or change, degrading segmentation temporal consistency and motion-boundary accuracy even though the input is objectively cleaner.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on compressed data will perform worse on raw captures than on matched-content compressed versions of the same captures, and the deficit will localize at motion boundaries where codec artifacts previously provided gradient structure, reversing the expected clean-data advantage.
why_important: The assumption that cleaner input helps underlies acquisition upgrades (raw workflows, new codecs); a codec-cue dependence means model behavior is tied to the encoding ecosystem, and codec migration (AV1 replacing H.264) will cause silent regressions.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compressed-domain vision exploits codec information deliberately; unintentional codec-cue dependence in pixel-domain segmentation models with clean-data regression appears undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public video segmenters on paired raw and compressed versions of identical clips, stratify by motion-boundary proximity, and test for the reverse gap.
main_risk: Truly raw video benchmarks are scarce; capture campaigns or lossless game-engine footage may be needed to construct the paired condition.
default_community_belief: Higher-quality, less-compressed input can only help models trained on compressed data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may rely predominantly on appearance and learned temporal features, with codec micro-artifacts contributing nothing that their removal would expose.
fastest_falsification: Raw-versus-compressed paired evaluation on one model and a small paired set, one day.

one_line: Temporal-consistency training installs persistence bias: consistency-optimized video segmenters are systematically late and inaccurate on object state changes.
problem: Temporal consistency losses and post-processing are near-universal in video segmentation, penalizing frame-to-frame change without distinguishing annotation noise from genuine object dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Consistency objectives teach models to distrust change, so masks lag deformations, splits, and appearance transitions; the smoothing gain on static content and the responsiveness loss on dynamic events are two ends of one tradeoff that current training pushes toward persistence, measurable as a systematic detection delay for state-change events.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched average accuracy, consistency-trained models will show significantly longer latencies and higher error around annotated state-change events (object splitting, rapid deformation, class transitions) than per-frame counterparts, with latency scaling with the consistency-loss weight.
why_important: Streaming applications exist to detect change (safety events, process transitions); optimizing benchmarks that reward smoothness selects models that are worst exactly at the moments that matter, a metric-deployment mismatch that needs quantification.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: temporal consistency is treated as unambiguously good; a persistence-versus-responsiveness dissociation with event-locked latency measurement appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models across consistency-weight settings on one video benchmark with annotated events, measure event-locked latency and error versus weight.
main_risk: Benchmarks with dense state-change annotations are rare; event annotation of a subset may be required before the main experiment.
default_community_belief: Temporal consistency improves video segmentation quality without meaningful downside.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern attention-based temporal models may achieve smoothness by better evidence integration rather than change suppression, escaping the tradeoff.
fastest_falsification: Event-locked latency comparison between one consistency-trained and one per-frame model, one day.

one_line: Temporal information for streaming segmentation saturates within a few frames: long-memory architectures buy identity persistence, not segmentation accuracy, and the two are conflated in benchmarks.
problem: Streaming segmentation invests heavily in long-range memory, justified by aggregate benchmark gains that mix mask-quality and identity-tracking contributions.
core_hypothesis: For pixel-level mask accuracy, usable temporal information saturates within a short horizon (order of several frames) because appearance decorrelates quickly; gains from long memory come almost entirely from instance-identity maintenance, so decomposed evaluation will show mask-quality gains flat beyond a short window while identity metrics keep improving.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating memory horizon in one architecture will show mask-quality metrics (per-frame IoU against identity-blind ground truth) plateauing at short horizons across datasets, while identity-sensitive metrics continue improving with horizon, dissociating the two contributions.
why_important: Compute budgets for streaming deployment are dominated by memory mechanisms; knowing that accuracy saturates early would redirect design toward cheap short-window models plus lightweight identity bookkeeping, and expose benchmark scores as identity-weighted rather than segmentation-weighted.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: memory ablations exist per paper; a systematic information-saturation decomposition separating mask quality from identity persistence appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Horizon-sweep ablation on one memory-based video segmenter with decomposed metrics on two benchmarks.
main_risk: Occlusion recovery genuinely needs long memory for mask quality in some scenes; the saturation claim must be stratified by occlusion statistics to be honest.
default_community_belief: Longer temporal memory improves video segmentation broadly, justifying its computational cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On occlusion-heavy footage the saturation horizon may be long enough that the distinction loses practical force.
fastest_falsification: Memory-horizon sweep with decomposed metrics on one public model, one day.

one_line: Video super-resolution creates mask flicker: per-frame quality improves while temporal instability of downstream segmentation exceeds that of the degraded input.
problem: Video SR is evaluated frame-wise or with temporal-quality metrics designed for human viewing; its effect on the temporal stability of downstream dense predictions is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: SR resolves per-frame ambiguity independently (or with limited temporal coupling), so fabricated details differ across frames, injecting high-frequency temporal noise; segmentation on SR output will show more mask flicker than segmentation on the un-super-resolved input, even as per-frame accuracy rises.
falsifiable_prediction: Flicker metrics (frame-to-frame mask change not explained by ground-truth motion) will be significantly higher for SR-then-segment than for segment-on-LR pipelines on matched content, with the excess flicker localized at hallucination-prone regions identified by cross-seed variance.
why_important: Temporal stability drives downstream tracking, counting, and human trust in overlays; a preprocessing step that improves stills while destabilizing sequences would be systematically mischosen by current frame-based selection criteria.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: temporal consistency of video SR is studied for visual flicker; propagation into downstream mask instability with hallucination-locality analysis appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run video SR plus frozen segmenter versus direct LR segmentation on one benchmark, compute motion-compensated mask-flicker metrics, and localize excess flicker against SR-variance maps.
main_risk: Motion-compensated flicker measurement requires accurate flow on degraded footage; flow errors must be bounded or ground-truth synthetic motion used.
default_community_belief: Video SR that improves per-frame quality improves, or at least does not harm, downstream video analysis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporally coupled SR architectures with alignment modules may already suppress fabrication variance below segmentation sensitivity.
fastest_falsification: Flicker comparison on one benchmark with one video SR model, one day.

one_line: Frame interpolation fabricates linear motion, so segmentation and tracking on interpolated video infer wrong occlusion order at object crossings.
problem: Frame interpolation is used to standardize frame rates and smooth footage before analysis, and its outputs are treated as observations; interpolators must guess inter-frame motion and depth ordering where objects cross.
core_hypothesis: Interpolators impose near-linear motion and learned occlusion priors, so at crossings they synthesize plausible but frequently wrong layering; segmentation on interpolated frames will assign occlusion boundaries to the wrong object at rates far above adjacent real frames, corrupting depth-order-sensitive downstream reasoning.
falsifiable_prediction: Using high-fps ground truth downsampled and re-interpolated, occlusion-order errors in segmented interpolated frames will significantly exceed those in matched real frames, concentrated at crossings with nonlinear true motion, and error rate will track the interpolator's motion-linearity assumption strength.
why_important: Interpolated frames are increasingly indistinguishable from real ones and enter analysis pipelines unlabeled; layered-scene errors at crossings propagate into tracking identity switches and interaction inference, a forensic and safety concern.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: interpolation quality is scored photometrically; occlusion-order fidelity at crossings as a downstream analysis property appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Downsample high-fps benchmarks, interpolate with two methods, segment, and score occlusion-order agreement against the withheld real frames at annotated crossings.
main_risk: Crossing events with ground-truth ordering are sparse; synthetic scenes with controlled crossings may be needed to reach statistical power.
default_community_belief: Good interpolation is analysis-neutral because photometric quality is high.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern interpolators with learned occlusion reasoning may handle typical crossings well enough that residual ordering errors are rare in natural footage.
fastest_falsification: Occlusion-order audit at crossings on one re-interpolated benchmark, one day.

one_line: Video diffusion restoration imposes object permanence beyond evidence: departed objects get regenerated, and downstream trackers report phantom re-identifications.
problem: Video diffusion models used for restoration and inpainting learn strong object-permanence priors from natural video; how these priors behave when objects genuinely leave the scene during degraded spans is untested.
core_hypothesis: When evidence is weak (occlusion, dropout, heavy noise), video diffusion restorers continue objects that plausibly should persist, re-synthesizing them after they actually departed; downstream segmentation and tracking then produce phantom object continuations with confident appearance, a failure class unique to generative temporal priors.
falsifiable_prediction: On constructed sequences where objects exit during degraded spans, generative restoration will re-instantiate departed objects at rates far above non-generative restoration baselines, and tracker outputs on the restored video will contain measurable phantom track continuations time-locked to the degraded spans.
why_important: Surveillance, autonomy, and scientific tracking rely on absence being detectable; a restoration stage that reifies expected-but-absent objects converts missing evidence into false positive presence, the most dangerous direction of error for these applications.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: video generation permanence is a modeling achievement; its inversion into a restoration hazard with tracker-level phantom quantification appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct exit-during-degradation sequences from real footage, restore with video diffusion and classical baselines, and count phantom re-instantiations plus downstream phantom tracks.
main_risk: Effect size depends on degradation severity and prior strength; a severity sweep is needed to map where the hazard becomes material.
default_community_belief: Restoration recovers what is there; the risk vocabulary covers distortion and blur, not confabulated object persistence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conditioning on surrounding clean frames may anchor the restorer to actual object absence, making phantoms rare outside extreme degradation.
fastest_falsification: Exit-scenario test with one public video diffusion restorer, one day.

one_line: Segmentation models silently correct rolling-shutter distortions of fast-moving objects toward canonical shapes, corrupting downstream geometry instead of reporting the distortion.
