problem: Rolling-shutter capture geometrically distorts fast movers (skewed wheels, bent propellers); how shape-prior-laden segmentation models respond to physically distorted but real object shapes is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on predominantly undistorted objects treat rolling-shutter shapes as noise and regularize masks toward canonical shapes, so mask geometry disagrees with actual pixel evidence in a velocity-dependent way; downstream geometric estimates (orientation, speed from shape) inherit hidden corrections that break physical consistency.
falsifiable_prediction: On rolling-shutter footage with global-shutter reference, mask-versus-pixel-evidence disagreement will grow with object velocity and shutter skew, in the direction of canonical shape restoration, and will be absent for global-shutter footage of the same scenes.
why_important: Vision-based measurement (speed enforcement, industrial inspection, drone analytics) assumes masks follow pixel evidence; prior-driven silent correction breaks the measurement chain in a way that looks like better segmentation on standard metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: rolling shutter is studied in geometry pipelines; segmentation-model shape-prior interaction with shutter distortion appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or source paired rolling/global-shutter footage of fast rotating and translating objects, segment, and measure evidence-mask disagreement versus velocity.
main_risk: Paired-shutter data is niche; synthetic shutter simulation on high-fps footage is the fallback, with realism caveats.
default_community_belief: Segmentation follows image evidence; shape priors only fill in ambiguity, they do not override visible geometry.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rolling-shutter shapes may be represented in modern training data (phone footage) well enough that models segment the distorted shapes faithfully.
fastest_falsification: Evidence-mask disagreement measurement on available rolling-shutter clips of rotating objects, one day.

one_line: Streaming memory segmenters amplify temporally correlated restoration errors: preprocessing that helps per-frame models destabilizes memory-based ones superlinearly.
problem: Restoration is validated with per-frame downstream metrics, but streaming segmenters carry state; the interaction between temporally correlated restoration errors and recurrent memory is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Restoration errors persist across frames (same hallucination re-rendered), so memory modules integrate them as confirmed evidence; error accumulates and locks into the state, making memory-based pipelines degrade with sequence length under restoration while per-frame pipelines stay flat, reversing the usual memory advantage.
falsifiable_prediction: On long degraded sequences, accuracy of memory-based segmenters fed restored frames will decline with sequence position significantly faster than per-frame baselines fed the same frames, and state-reset interventions will recover accuracy stepwise, confirming state contamination as the mechanism.
why_important: The two most common upgrades to video pipelines (restoration preprocessing and temporal memory) may be antagonistic; system designers currently combine them freely, and the interaction is invisible in short-clip benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: error accumulation in tracking is known; restoration-correlated-error interaction with segmentation memory, with reset-based causal confirmation, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Feed one memory-based and one per-frame segmenter identical restored long sequences, plot accuracy versus position, and apply periodic state resets to test the mechanism.
main_risk: Long-sequence annotated benchmarks are scarce; semi-automatic ground truth from high-quality originals is needed for the degraded-restored condition.
default_community_belief: Preprocessing quality gains and temporal memory gains are independent and additive in video pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Memory architectures with appearance-based confidence gating may reject inconsistent restored content, keeping accumulation subcritical.
fastest_falsification: Position-resolved accuracy comparison on one long benchmark, one day.

one_line: Auto-exposure transients cause time-locked segmentation dropouts that shuffled-frame evaluation cannot detect, making deployed streaming accuracy lower than benchmarked accuracy.
problem: Cameras adapt exposure abruptly at illumination changes (doorways, headlights, cloud edges); benchmarks curate stable footage and evaluate frames independently, so adaptation transients are absent from the measurement.
core_hypothesis: During exposure transitions, image statistics traverse regions poorly covered by training data (global gain ramps, temporary clipping), causing brief but severe segmentation dropouts time-locked to adaptation events; deployed streams encounter such events frequently, creating a benchmark-deployment accuracy gap concentrated in temporally localized bursts.
falsifiable_prediction: Event-locked analysis on footage with logged exposure changes will show accuracy dips of large magnitude within a fixed window after adaptation onset, recovering to baseline afterward, with total deployed-accuracy impact proportional to event frequency, and standard benchmarks will show near-zero such events.
why_important: Burst failures at illumination transitions coincide with safety-relevant moments (entering tunnels, doors opening); quantifying this hidden failure mode reframes robustness from average-case severity to event-locked dynamics and motivates exposure-transient augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: illumination robustness is studied as static severity; exposure-adaptation transients as time-locked failure events with frequency accounting appear unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect or identify footage with exposure metadata, run frozen segmenters, and compute event-locked accuracy curves plus benchmark event-frequency audits.
main_risk: Ground truth during transients is hard to annotate due to genuine visibility loss; human-visibility-controlled scoring windows are needed to separate model failure from information absence.
default_community_belief: Robustness benchmarks with photometric corruptions adequately cover illumination-related failure modes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern imaging stacks smooth exposure transitions well enough that transients may be too brief to affect analytics meaningfully.
fastest_falsification: Event-locked accuracy analysis on dashcam footage with detectable exposure steps, two days.

one_line: Distilling per-frame pseudo-labels into video models amplifies flicker-consistent errors: mistakes that happen to be temporally stable get promoted to confident learned structure.
problem: Video segmentation training increasingly uses per-frame image-model pseudo-labels aggregated with temporal consistency filtering, assuming temporal stability separates correct labels from errors.
core_hypothesis: Consistency filtering removes random errors but selects for systematic ones (persistent misclassification of specific objects), so the distilled video model inherits a purified set of stable errors and reproduces them with high confidence; the pseudo-label pipeline transforms error character from noisy to structural.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing teacher errors with distilled-student errors will show random teacher errors largely absent in the student while temporally stable teacher errors survive at high rates and gain confidence, producing student error profiles more concentrated and confident than the teacher's on identical content.
why_important: The pseudo-label-then-distill recipe is the dominant path to scaling video segmentation without annotation; understanding that it selectively amplifies systematic teacher defects predicts where the resulting foundation-style video models will be confidently wrong.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: pseudo-label noise is studied generically; the selection-for-stable-errors mechanism specific to temporal-consistency filtering appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the standard distillation recipe on one benchmark with known ground truth, partition teacher errors by temporal stability, and measure differential survival and confidence in the student.
main_risk: Stable teacher errors may correlate with genuinely ambiguous content where ground truth is itself soft, requiring multi-annotator reference for interpretation.
default_community_belief: Temporal consistency filtering of pseudo-labels improves their quality and hence the distilled model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Diverse teacher ensembles may decorrelate systematic errors enough that stability filtering keeps mostly correct labels after all.
fastest_falsification: Stability-partitioned error-survival analysis on an existing distillation pipeline, one day.

one_line: Duplicate frames and variable frame rates in web training video teach a spurious zero-motion prior: slow-moving objects are under-segmented relative to static ones of identical appearance.
problem: Web video corpora contain frozen frames, duplicated frames from rate conversion, and variable timing, which distort the motion statistics that video models internalize.
core_hypothesis: Duplicate-heavy training data over-represents exact-zero motion, creating a prior gap between zero and small motion; models therefore handle static objects and fast movers well but under-segment the slow-motion band where the learned motion distribution has an artifactual notch.
falsifiable_prediction: Speed-stratified evaluation with appearance controls will show a recall dip specifically in the slow-motion band for models trained on web video, absent for models trained on rate-verified footage, and the dip location will track the duplicate-frame statistics of each training corpus.
why_important: Slow-moving content includes safety-critical categories (pedestrians drifting, machinery creeping); a training-data-artifact recall dip in exactly that band is a concrete deployment hazard invisible to aggregate metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: corpus timing defects are known to data engineers; their causal link to a speed-band segmentation deficit appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Audit duplicate statistics of one training corpus, evaluate the corresponding public model with speed-stratified metrics, and retrain a small model on deduplicated data as the causal check.
main_risk: Speed stratification requires reliable ground-truth motion; benchmarks with tracked annotations or synthetic control footage are prerequisites.
default_community_belief: Web-scale video diversity averages out timing artifacts, leaving learned motion priors faithful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optical-flow-conditioned architectures may bypass learned motion priors, confining the effect to purely appearance-temporal models.
fastest_falsification: Speed-stratified recall analysis on one public model and tracked benchmark, one day.

one_line: Event cameras contribute boundary re-localization rather than object discovery to segmentation: fusion gains decompose almost entirely into boundary-metric improvements.
problem: Event-frame fusion for segmentation reports aggregate gains attributed broadly to the event stream's temporal resolution and dynamic range, without decomposing what information events actually add.
core_hypothesis: Events are edge-triggered and carry little region-interior evidence, so their contribution is precise boundary timing and localization on moving objects; decomposition will show fusion improving boundary F-scores strongly while leaving region-discovery metrics (object-level recall of unmoving or texture-defined objects) unchanged, defining a narrow but sharp utility envelope for the modality.
falsifiable_prediction: Metric-decomposed ablations across fusion architectures will show event contributions concentrated in boundary displacement and temporal-lag metrics for moving-object boundaries, with statistically negligible contribution to interior-region accuracy or static-object recall.
why_important: Sensor-suite design for embedded segmentation needs to know what each modality buys; if events buy only boundary sharpness on movers, cheaper alternatives (higher frame rate, better deblurring) can be evaluated against that specific contribution rather than a vague fusion gain.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: event-fusion papers report aggregate benchmark improvements; a contribution-decomposition account with a falsifiable narrow-envelope claim appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one event-fusion segmentation model, ablate the event stream, and decompose the metric change into boundary, interior, and detection components across motion strata.
main_risk: Decomposition results may be architecture-specific; at least two fusion designs are needed before claiming a modality-level property.
default_community_belief: Event streams add broad robustness and information to segmentation under fast motion and challenging lighting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In extreme low light the frame stream may be so degraded that events carry region evidence too, widening their contribution beyond boundaries.
fastest_falsification: Ablation with decomposed metrics on one public event-fusion model, one day.

one_line: Streaming segmentation rankings are hardware-coupled: accuracy-latency Pareto fronts cross between GPUs, so published real-time claims do not transfer across devices.
problem: Real-time video segmentation methods are ranked by accuracy at a latency budget measured on one hardware platform, treating the ranking as a property of the algorithms.
core_hypothesis: Architectural choices (attention versus convolution, memory access patterns, dynamic computation) scale differently across hardware generations and classes, so accuracy-latency Pareto fronts of competing methods cross between devices; the real-time ranking is a joint property of method and hardware, and single-device leaderboards mispredict deployment choices.
falsifiable_prediction: Benchmarking a set of published streaming segmenters across three hardware classes (server GPU, embedded GPU, CPU) will produce at least one Pareto-rank inversion between devices at common latency budgets, with inversion structure explained by operator-level profiling.
why_important: Deployment decisions and research directions follow leaderboards; if rankings invert across hardware, the field's real-time claims need device-conditional reporting, and method development is being steered by one vendor's current architecture.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: hardware-dependent throughput is obvious to engineers; a systematic Pareto-crossing audit for streaming segmentation with profiling attribution appears unpublished as a scientific claim about benchmark validity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross-device benchmark of five methods with matched software stacks, Pareto-front construction per device, and inversion analysis.
main_risk: Software-stack optimization maturity differs across devices and frameworks; results must control for compilation and kernel optimization effort to isolate architectural effects.
default_community_belief: Real-time segmentation rankings measured on standard research GPUs generalize to deployment hardware.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rank differences may be small and confined to latency regimes no application actually uses, making the inversion academically real but practically irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: Two-device Pareto comparison of three methods, two days including setup.

one_line: Restoration and segmentation benchmarks share source imagery, so restoration models can memorize the clean versions of segmentation test images, silently inflating restoration-utility studies.
problem: Restoration training corpora and segmentation benchmarks both draw from the same public image pools; a restorer that saw a test image's clean version during training performs reconstruction from memory, not restoration, but utility studies never audit this overlap.
core_hypothesis: Cross-task duplicate rates between popular restoration training sets and segmentation benchmark test sets are nonzero and material; on overlapping images, restoration quality and downstream segmentation utility are anomalously high, biasing conclusions about how much restoration helps segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: Embedding-based duplicate retrieval will find measurable overlap between at least one major restoration training corpus and one segmentation benchmark, and restoration-then-segmentation utility on overlapping images will exceed utility on matched non-overlapping images by a significant margin.
why_important: Restoration-utility experiments guide pipeline design decisions; memorization-inflated utility would overstate the case for generative preprocessing exactly on the benchmarks the community trusts most, and the audit protocol generalizes to any cross-task contamination question.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: within-task contamination is studied; cross-task contamination between restoration corpora and segmentation benchmarks appears unaudited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run duplicate retrieval between one restoration corpus and one segmentation test set, then compare utility metrics on overlapping versus matched non-overlapping subsets.
main_risk: Popular benchmarks may have small overlaps, limiting statistical power; the audit is still valuable as a bound even with a null result.
default_community_belief: Contamination checks within a task suffice; models from a different task pose no memorization threat to evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration training pipelines that crop aggressively may prevent whole-image memorization, weakening per-image utility inflation even when overlap exists.
fastest_falsification: Duplicate retrieval between one corpus pair, hours with precomputed embeddings.

one_line: Synthetic-corruption robustness rankings mispredict real-degradation robustness rankings: the rank correlation across model families is weak enough to invalidate corruption suites as selection tools.
problem: Corruption benchmarks with synthetic noise, blur, and weather are the standard instrument for comparing segmentation robustness, and model selection for deployment follows these rankings without validation against real degradation.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic corruptions differ from real degradations in noise correlation structure, ISP interaction, and semantics-degradation coupling, so model rankings on corruption suites and on genuinely degraded imagery diverge substantially, especially across architecture families that interact differently with the synthetic artifact structure.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a diverse model pool on a synthetic corruption suite and on paired real degraded data (real fog, real low light, real motion blur with clean references) will yield cross-benchmark rank correlations low enough that top-third selection by synthetic ranking misses the real-data winner in a substantial fraction of degradation types.
why_important: If the field's robustness instrument mis-ranks models, years of robustness progress claims and deployment decisions rest on a miscalibrated measurement; quantifying the miscalibration per degradation type tells the community where synthetic suites remain valid.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: individual synthetic-real gaps are documented; a systematic rank-transfer audit across model families and degradation types for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble paired real-degradation segmentation data for three degradation types, evaluate ten public models plus the corruption suite, and compute rank-transfer statistics.
main_risk: Real degraded data with segmentation labels is scarce; label transfer from clean references must be validated to avoid annotation confounds.
default_community_belief: Corruption-suite robustness is a valid proxy for real-world degradation robustness at the model-ranking level.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rankings may be dominated by general model capability, which transfers across both benchmark types, keeping correlations high despite artifact mismatch.
fastest_falsification: Rank comparison on one real-degradation dataset with existing checkpoints, one day.

one_line: Evaluating restored-image segmentation against clean-image ground truth credits hallucination: an evidence-limited ground-truth protocol flips method rankings.
problem: When segmentation is evaluated on restored images, the reference masks come from the original clean scene, so a model gets full credit for segmenting structures the degraded input contained no evidence for, as long as the restorer guessed them correctly by prior.
core_hypothesis: Current protocols conflate evidence-based accuracy with prior-guessing accuracy; scoring against evidence-limited references (what is recoverable from the degraded input, operationalized by human performance or information-theoretic bounds) will systematically re-rank restoration-segmentation pipelines, demoting prior-heavy generative pipelines and promoting evidence-faithful ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing evidence-limited references for one degraded benchmark will produce pipeline rankings that differ from clean-reference rankings, with generative restorers losing the most rank, and the ranking difference will exceed evaluation noise.
why_important: The measurement question determines what the field optimizes: clean-reference evaluation actively rewards confident guessing, steering restoration research toward hallucination; an evidence-referenced protocol realigns benchmarks with deployment risk.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the guessing-credit problem is occasionally noted informally; a constructed evidence-limited evaluation protocol with demonstrated rank flips appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build evidence-limited references via human segmentation of degraded inputs on a benchmark subset, score pipelines under both protocols, and compare rankings.
main_risk: Human performance on degraded inputs is a lower bound on recoverable information, not a tight one; the protocol needs sensitivity analysis to the reference construction method.
default_community_belief: Clean-scene ground truth is the correct reference regardless of what preprocessing produced the evaluated image.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For many applications, being right for prior reasons is operationally as good as being right for evidence reasons, making the clean-reference protocol defensible for those use cases.
fastest_falsification: Pilot with human annotation of 100 degraded images and dual-protocol scoring, days.

one_line: Boundary metrics are not resolution-invariant: evaluating the same predictions at different resolutions re-ranks methods, and SR-and-restoration papers implicitly exploit favorable evaluation scales.
problem: Boundary F-scores and surface distances depend on the pixel grid at which they are computed, yet papers evaluate at heterogeneous, often unreported resolutions, especially in SR contexts where output and reference scales differ by construction.
core_hypothesis: Boundary-metric tolerance bands scale with pixel size, so computing metrics at output resolution versus reference resolution changes both absolute scores and method orderings; SR-segmentation papers evaluating at upscaled resolution gain a systematic advantage invisible to readers, making cross-paper boundary claims incommensurable.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing published-style boundary metrics for fixed predictions across evaluation resolutions will show method-rank changes at competitive margins and a directional advantage for evaluating at higher resolution with fixed-pixel tolerance, quantifiable as an inflation factor per resolution ratio.
why_important: Boundary quality is where modern methods differentiate; an unpinned evaluation-scale convention corrupts exactly the field's finest-grained comparisons and provides a concrete standardization fix (physical-unit or reference-scale tolerance).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: metric implementation sensitivity is folklore; a quantified resolution-dependence law with cross-paper inflation analysis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take fixed predictions from several models, sweep evaluation resolution and tolerance conventions, and map score inflation and rank changes.
main_risk: The study must carefully separate resampling-of-predictions effects from metric-grid effects, or the conclusion conflates two mechanisms.
default_community_belief: Boundary metrics computed with standard tools are comparable across papers up to minor implementation noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If most papers happen to use one dominant toolchain and scale, de facto standardization may already limit the damage to SR-adjacent niches.
fastest_falsification: Resolution-sweep metric recomputation on cached predictions, hours.

one_line: Generalized energy distance rewards degenerate diversity: adding structured noise samples improves GED scores for multi-sample segmentation without adding any valid interpretation.
problem: GED and similar distribution metrics are the standard for evaluating ambiguity-aware segmentation, assumed to reward matching the annotator distribution; their gameability by degenerate sample sets is uncharacterized in this domain.
core_hypothesis: Because GED trades off self-distance against cross-distance, sample sets padded with boundary-jittered or partially corrupted variants can lower GED relative to honest concentrated predictions, even when the added samples correspond to no plausible annotation; the metric therefore cannot distinguish calibrated ambiguity from engineered dispersion.
falsifiable_prediction: For fixed base predictions on multi-rater benchmarks, algorithmically constructed padding samples (jitter, dropout of components) will improve GED significantly while human raters judge the padded sets as containing invalid masks, and a mode-coverage-based alternative will resist the same manipulation.
why_important: Papers claim ambiguity modeling superiority via GED margins; demonstrating a constructive gaming procedure invalidates those margins as evidence and forces the subfield toward manipulation-resistant evaluation, directly affecting how diffusion-segmentation diversity claims are assessed.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: metric gaming is demonstrated in other fields; a constructive GED-gaming result for segmentation with a proposed resistance criterion appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement padding strategies on top of one published multi-sample method, measure GED gains, run a small human validity study on padded samples, and test alternative metrics for resistance.
main_risk: The demonstration must avoid strawman padding: strategies should be constrained to what a motivated method author could plausibly ship inside a model.
default_community_belief: Lower GED against annotator distributions means better ambiguity modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On well-annotated benchmarks the exploitable gap between honest and gamed GED may be small, making the vulnerability theoretical rather than practical.
fastest_falsification: Jitter-padding GED experiment on one public multi-rater benchmark, hours.

one_line: Sparse annotation cadence in video benchmarks rewards persistence-biased models: dense re-annotation of even short spans flips method rankings toward event-responsive models.
problem: Video segmentation benchmarks annotate every Nth frame for cost reasons; the sampling interacts with model temporal biases, since persistence errors between annotated frames go unmeasured while responsiveness errors on annotated frames are penalized.
core_hypothesis: Sparse cadence systematically undercounts the errors of temporally over-smoothed models (which fail between annotations during dynamics) relative to responsive models (whose jitter is fully visible on annotated frames), so current rankings favor persistence bias; densely annotated evaluation spans will show ranking reversals during dynamic content.
falsifiable_prediction: Densely re-annotating short dynamic spans of one benchmark and re-scoring published methods will significantly change method orderings relative to sparse-cadence scores, in the direction of penalizing temporally smoothed models, with the effect concentrated in high-dynamics spans.
why_important: Annotation cadence is an economic choice silently acting as a metric design choice; demonstrating cadence-dependent rankings would change how video benchmarks allocate annotation budgets (dense spans versus uniform sparse) and re-interpret existing leaderboards.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotation sparsity is discussed as a cost issue; its systematic interaction with model temporal bias as a ranking distortion appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Densely annotate dynamic spans in one benchmark, re-score public methods under both cadences, and test for the predicted rank shifts.
main_risk: Dense annotation is expensive; span selection must be motion-stratified but blinded to model outputs to avoid selection bias.
default_community_belief: Sparse-frame evaluation is an unbiased subsample of dense evaluation for ranking purposes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If dynamics-heavy frames are rare in realistic footage, sparse and dense rankings may agree in the aggregate even if they diverge on dynamic spans.
fastest_falsification: Simulation study downsampling an existing densely annotated benchmark to sparse cadences and measuring rank stability, hours.

one_line: Reported diffusion-segmentation advantages shrink or vanish under compute-matched comparison: multi-step sampling budgets, given to discriminative ensembles, close most published gaps.
problem: Diffusion-based segmentation methods are compared against single-pass discriminative baselines despite spending many function evaluations per prediction, conflating paradigm benefits with inference-compute benefits.
core_hypothesis: A substantial share of published diffusion-segmentation improvements is purchasable by giving equal inference compute to discriminative models (ensembles, test-time augmentation, recurrent refinement); compute-matched re-evaluation will eliminate or reverse many headline gaps, isolating the residual as the paradigm's true contribution.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-running representative published comparisons with FLOP-matched or latency-matched baselines will reduce the median reported improvement substantially, with at least some comparisons flipping sign, and the residual paradigm advantage concentrating in distribution-modeling metrics rather than point-prediction accuracy.
why_important: Paradigm claims steer research investment; separating compute effects from modeling effects is basic measurement hygiene the diffusion-segmentation literature currently lacks, and the result calibrates how much the field should reallocate toward generative segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compute-matching critiques exist in other subfields; a systematic compute-matched audit of diffusion segmentation claims appears not yet performed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select three published comparisons with available code, construct FLOP-matched discriminative baselines (deep ensembles, TTA), and re-run the comparisons.
main_risk: Matching compute fairly is contested (training versus inference, memory versus FLOPs); results should be reported across several matching conventions to be robust.
default_community_belief: Published diffusion-segmentation gains reflect the value of generative modeling for dense prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For ambiguity-modeling tasks, no amount of discriminative ensembling may replicate the conditional-distribution quality, leaving the paradigm advantage intact where it matters.
fastest_falsification: TTA-and-ensemble compute-matched rerun of one published comparison, two days.

one_line: Ground-truth quality co-varies with image quality: annotations on degraded images are noisier, so measured robustness curves conflate model degradation with reference degradation.
problem: Robustness studies score models on degraded images against annotations made on those same degraded images (or transferred imperfectly from clean versions), never partitioning the accuracy drop into model failure versus reference failure.
core_hypothesis: Annotator accuracy and consistency fall with image quality, so a nontrivial fraction of the measured model-accuracy drop under degradation is reference noise, inflating robustness pessimism and distorting comparisons whenever methods differ in their error correlation with annotator error.
falsifiable_prediction: Multi-annotator studies on degraded images will show inter-annotator agreement falling with severity, and correcting model scores with annotator-noise models will recover a significant fraction of the apparent robustness drop, changing the shape of published-style severity-accuracy curves.
why_important: Robustness numbers guide safety cases; overestimating model degradation misallocates engineering effort, and reference-noise correction methodology transfers to every degraded-image benchmark the field maintains.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotator noise is studied on clean data; its severity-dependence and impact on robustness-curve interpretation appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect multi-annotator labels across severity levels on one benchmark subset, model annotator noise versus severity, and re-estimate corrected robustness curves for public models.
main_risk: Separating genuine ambiguity growth from annotator error growth requires care; both increase with degradation but have different correction implications.
default_community_belief: Measured accuracy drops under degradation reflect model limitations against a fixed-quality reference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For moderately degraded images annotator performance may be nearly intact, confining the reference-noise effect to severities beyond practical interest.
fastest_falsification: Small multi-annotator pilot at three severity levels, days including annotation.

one_line: Tile-level i.i.d. aggregation in WSI and large-image benchmarks understates variance because errors cluster spatially, making many published significance claims unsupported.
problem: Gigapixel evaluations aggregate per-tile or per-patch metrics as independent samples, but errors cluster by slide region (focus, stain, seams, tissue architecture), violating independence exactly where restoration and scanner artifacts operate.
core_hypothesis: Effective sample sizes are far smaller than tile counts due to spatial error correlation; recomputing uncertainty with cluster-aware methods (slide-level or region-block bootstrap) will widen confidence intervals enough that a meaningful fraction of published-style method differences lose statistical significance.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring spatial autocorrelation of errors on WSI benchmarks will show correlation lengths spanning many tiles, and cluster-corrected re-analysis of typical method comparisons will flip a nontrivial fraction of significant differences to non-significant, with the flip rate predictable from correlation length.
why_important: Statistical practice determines which methods the field believes are better; systematically overconfident intervals in gigapixel evaluation would mean the pathology-AI literature contains an excess of spurious method distinctions, fixable by a standard reporting change.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: clustered-data statistics are standard elsewhere; an empirical audit of spatial error correlation and its significance impact in WSI segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute error autocorrelation on one WSI benchmark, run naive versus cluster-aware bootstrap on several model comparisons, and report the significance flip rate.
main_risk: Choice of clustering unit (slide, region, patient) changes corrections; the analysis should present a hierarchy rather than one arbitrary level.
default_community_belief: Tile counts in gigapixel benchmarks provide ample statistical power, making significance testing a formality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For some benchmarks, between-slide variance may already dominate and be handled by slide-level splits, leaving naive intervals roughly correct.
fastest_falsification: Error-autocorrelation measurement plus dual bootstrap on one benchmark, one day.

one_line: Human preference for restored images reverses with viewing zoom, and machine-utility correlates only with preferences collected at 1:1 pixel scale, invalidating fit-to-screen crowd studies.
problem: Crowdsourced restoration preference studies let raters view images fit-to-screen, but restoration differences (hallucinated texture, micro-artifacts) are scale-dependent, and downstream models consume full-resolution pixels.
core_hypothesis: Preference judgments flip between fit-to-screen and 1:1 viewing for a substantial fraction of restoration pairs (smoothness wins zoomed out, fidelity wins at native scale), and only native-scale preferences track downstream segmentation utility, so the field's dominant preference-collection protocol measures the wrong construct for pipeline decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled dual-condition preference study will show significant preference reversal rates between zoom conditions on restoration pairs, with the 1:1 condition's preferences correlating significantly better with frozen-segmenter utility than the fit-to-screen condition's.
why_important: Preference data trains and validates perceptual metrics and reward models now used to tune restorers; if the collection protocol biases toward zoom-out smoothness, the entire metric-training pipeline inherits an anti-fidelity bias with downstream consequences for machine consumers.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: viewing-condition effects are known in psychophysics; their quantified impact on restoration preference datasets and utility correlation appears undocumented in the learned-metric literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a within-subject dual-zoom preference study on restoration pairs with known downstream utility, and compare reversal rates and utility correlations across conditions.
main_risk: Zoom conditions change task difficulty and rater attention; the design needs attention checks and counterbalancing to attribute reversals to scale rather than effort.
default_community_belief: Crowd preference at convenient viewing scales is a stable ground truth for restoration quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Preference reversals may be confined to a small set of artifact types, leaving aggregate protocol conclusions intact.
fastest_falsification: Small dual-zoom pilot on 50 restoration pairs, days.

one_line: Restoration-utility rankings are evaluator-specific: which restorer is best for segmentation depends on the segmenter used to measure utility, with low rank correlation across evaluators.
problem: Task-utility evaluations of restoration methods use one downstream segmenter as the measuring instrument, and conclusions are stated as if utility were a property of the restorer alone.
core_hypothesis: Restorers and segmenters interact through matched or mismatched feature sensitivities (frequency preferences, color statistics, artifact tolerances), so utility rankings of restorers vary substantially across evaluator segmenters; a single-evaluator utility study measures a pairing, not a restorer property, and evaluator ensembles are necessary for transferable conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: Crossing a pool of restorers with a pool of diverse segmenters will yield restorer rank correlations across evaluators low enough that the best restorer under one evaluator falls outside the top third under another, with interaction variance comparable to restorer main-effect variance.
why_important: Pipeline builders read utility papers to choose preprocessing; if conclusions do not transfer across downstream models, the literature's recommendations are silently conditional, and utility benchmarking needs multi-evaluator protocols analogous to cross-validation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: evaluator dependence is occasionally acknowledged; a variance-decomposition study quantifying restorer-by-segmenter interaction appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate six restorers under six diverse frozen segmenters on one degraded benchmark and decompose utility variance into main effects and interaction.
main_risk: Diversity of the segmenter pool determines the result; the pool must span architectures and training data to avoid understating interaction.
default_community_belief: Task utility measured with a reasonable downstream model characterizes the restoration method itself.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If utility is dominated by evidence recovery common to all consumers, interaction variance will be small and single-evaluator studies vindicated.
fastest_falsification: Six-by-six crossing with existing checkpoints, two days of inference.

one_line: Temporal-quality metrics for video restoration do not predict downstream tracking and segmentation stability: the two notions of temporal consistency are measurably different constructs.
problem: Video restoration papers report temporal-consistency metrics (warping error, flicker indices) as evidence of downstream suitability, assuming visual temporal quality and analytic temporal stability coincide.
core_hypothesis: Visual temporal metrics penalize photometric flicker that analytics ignore, while missing semantic instability (structure identity changes between frames) that analytics catastrophically inherit; correlation between temporal-quality scores and downstream mask or track stability across restorers will be weak, and specific restorers will rank oppositely under the two measurement families.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of video restorers, rank correlation between warping-error-style metrics and downstream mask-stability or identity-switch metrics will be low, with identifiable restorer pairs ordered oppositely, and the divergence will be explained by semantic-instability events invisible to photometric metrics.
why_important: Video restoration is increasingly consumed by machines, and the community's temporal metrics were designed for human flicker perception; demonstrating construct divergence forces the development of analytics-referenced temporal metrics before restored video enters tracking-critical systems.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: metric-utility divergence is documented for spatial quality; the temporal analogue for video restoration and downstream segmentation appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several video restorers under both metric families on one benchmark with tracking annotations and compute rank correlations plus divergence case analysis.
main_risk: Downstream stability depends on the analytic model choice; using two or three diverse downstream models guards against evaluator-specific conclusions.
default_community_belief: Good temporal-consistency scores certify restored video for downstream temporal analysis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern learned temporal metrics may already capture semantic instability, making the divergence smaller than hypothesized for recent metric generations.
fastest_falsification: Dual-family metric comparison over public video restoration outputs, one day.
